glossary.gloss: The ancient Roman poet (70–19 BC), author of the Aeneid, who appears as a shade and becomes Dante's guide through Hell and Purgatory. He stands for human reason and the best of pagan wisdom, and was sent to rescue Dante at Beatrice's request.
A region of northern Italy. Virgil names it as the homeland of his parents.
People of Mantua, a city in Lombardy near where Virgil was born. He identifies himself as a Mantuan.
Julius Caesar, the Roman general and dictator (100–44 BC). Virgil says he was born late in Caesar's day.
The first Roman emperor (63 BC–14 AD), under whom Virgil lived and wrote. Dante calls him 'the good Augustus.'
The mortal father of Aeneas. Virgil's epic, the Aeneid, sang of Anchises's 'just son' who fled the burning of Troy.
The ancient city destroyed by the Greeks in the Trojan War. Aeneas escaped its fall and sailed to Italy.
Another name for Troy, here the citadel of the city, which was burned to the ground.
A mysterious savior-figure Virgil prophesies will hunt down the she-wolf (greed) and drive it back to Hell. His exact identity is left deliberately obscure.
A warrior-maiden of the Volscians in Virgil's Aeneid who died fighting the Trojans in Italy. Named among those who died in the wars over Italy's future.
A young Trojan warrior in the Aeneid, killed alongside his friend Nisus. Named among those who died of their wounds for Italy.
King of the Rutulians in the Aeneid and Aeneas's chief rival for Italy and the hand of Lavinia; he is killed by Aeneas. Named among the Italian war dead.
A Trojan warrior in the Aeneid, devoted friend of Euryalus; the two die together on a night raid. Named among the fallen.
The realm of the eternally damned through which Virgil leads Dante. Its souls cry out in grief, each screaming for 'a second death.'
Virgil's reverent name for God, who reigns above and rules the universe from his high throne. As a pagan, Virgil rebelled against (never knew) his law, so he may not enter God's city.
The apostle and first pope, here the gatekeeper of Heaven. Dante asks to be led to 'the gate of Saint Peter.'
The nine goddesses of poetry and the arts in Greek and Roman myth, invoked by poets for inspiration. Dante calls on them at the start of his journey.
The son of Aeneas. Dante refers to Aeneas as 'the father of Silvius,' recalling that Aeneas visited the underworld while still alive.
The Trojan hero of Virgil's Aeneid who fled Troy, descended living into the underworld, and founded the line that led to Rome. Dante measures himself against him: 'I am not Aeneas.'
The great city Aeneas's descendants founded, destined in Dante's view to be the seat of empire and of the papacy ('where the heir of greatest Peter sits').
Saint Paul, called the 'chosen vessel' in Acts. Tradition held he too was caught up to the otherworld; Dante pairs him with Aeneas as a living visitor to the beyond.
Dante's idealized beloved, now a blessed soul in Heaven. Out of love and pity she comes down to Limbo to send Virgil to rescue Dante; she represents divine grace and revelation.
Saint Lucy, an early Christian martyr associated with sight and illumination, and Dante's special patron. In Heaven she urges Beatrice to help Dante.
The biblical wife of Jacob, here a blessed soul seated beside Beatrice in Heaven; she traditionally symbolizes the contemplative life. (She also appears among the souls Christ frees from Limbo.)
The Virgin Mary, never named directly in Hell, whose mercy sets the whole rescue of Dante in motion. She grieves at his peril and calls on Lucy.
The first river of the underworld, whose dismal shore the damned must cross by Charon's ferry to enter Hell proper.

glossary.term: the one who made the great refusal
glossary.gloss: A shade among the indifferent, traditionally identified as Pope Celestine V, who resigned the papacy 'out of cowardice,' opening the way for Boniface VIII.
The grim ferryman of the dead who carries damned souls across the river Acheron, with wheels of flame around his eyes. He beats the lingering souls with his oar.
The first man of the Bible. Dante calls the damned souls 'the evil seed of Adam,' the corrupted human race.
The first circle of Hell, holding the virtuous unbaptized and the noble pagans. They suffer no torment, only an endless longing for God they can never reach.
Christ, who after his crucifixion descended into Limbo (the 'Harrowing of Hell') and led out the worthy souls of the Old Testament. Virgil saw him 'crowned with the sign of victory.'
The second son of Adam, murdered by his brother Cain. Among the biblical souls Christ rescues from Limbo.
The biblical patriarch who built the ark and survived the Flood. Among those Christ draws out of Limbo.
The biblical prophet and lawgiver who led Israel out of Egypt. Named among the saved souls of Limbo as 'Moses the lawgiver.'
The biblical patriarch, father of the Hebrew people. Among the souls Christ frees from Limbo.
The biblical king of Israel and psalmist. Named 'David the king' among the rescued souls of Limbo.
Another name for Jacob, son of Isaac and father of the twelve tribes. Listed 'with his father and his sons' among those Christ leads from Limbo.
The greatest of the ancient Greek poets, author of the Iliad and Odyssey. In Limbo he leads the company of poets, sword in hand as 'sovereign poet of them all.'
The Roman lyric and satiric poet (65–8 BC). Named among the four great poets Dante meets in Limbo, 'Horace, the satirist.'
The Roman poet (43 BC–17 AD), author of the Metamorphoses, a key source for Dante. One of the great poets in Limbo.
The Roman epic poet (39–65 AD), author of the Pharsalia on Rome's civil war. The fourth of the great poets Dante joins in Limbo.
In Dante a Trojan ancestress (mother of Dardanus, founder of Troy's line), seen in Limbo surrounded by Trojan and Roman heroes.
The greatest Trojan warrior, killed by Achilles in the Iliad. Seen among the noble souls of Limbo.
Julius Caesar, the Roman general and statesman, here shown in Limbo 'armed, with his hawk's keen eyes.'
Queen of the Amazons who fought for Troy and was killed by Achilles. Seen with Camilla among the heroic souls of Limbo.
The king of Latium in the Aeneid who gives his daughter Lavinia to Aeneas. Seated in Limbo with his daughter.
Daughter of King Latinus and the bride of Aeneas in the Aeneid, ancestress of the Roman line. Seen seated with her father in Limbo.
Lucius Junius Brutus, who drove out the last king Tarquin and founded the Roman Republic. (Not the later Brutus who killed Caesar.) Seen in Limbo.
Tarquin the Proud, the last king of Rome, expelled by Brutus to found the Republic.
A noble Roman woman whose violation and suicide sparked the overthrow of the kings. Among the virtuous Roman souls in Limbo.
Daughter of Julius Caesar and wife of Pompey, a symbol of Roman virtue. Seen among the women of Limbo.
The wife of Cato the Younger, a model of Roman matronly virtue. Among the noble souls of Limbo.
A revered Roman matron, mother of the Gracchi, famed for her virtue. Seen among the women in Limbo.
The Muslim sultan (1137–1193) who fought the Crusaders, admired in the Middle Ages for his generosity and nobility. He sits 'alone and apart' in Limbo.

glossary.term: the master of those who know
glossary.gloss: Aristotle, the supreme philosopher in Dante's eyes, seated among his 'family of philosophers' in Limbo, honored by all.
The Athenian philosopher (469–399 BC), teacher of Plato. He stands nearest to Aristotle in Limbo.
The Athenian philosopher (c. 428–348 BC), student of Socrates. Among the closest to Aristotle in Limbo.
The early Greek philosopher who held the world arose from atoms and chance ('lays the world to chance'). Seen in Limbo.
The Greek Cynic philosopher famed for his rejection of convention. Among the thinkers in Limbo.
An early Greek philosopher who taught that mind orders the cosmos. Listed among the philosophers of Limbo.
One of the earliest Greek philosophers, who held water to be the first principle of things. Seen in Limbo.
A Greek philosopher (likely Zeno of Elea or of Citium) named among the thinkers in Limbo.
The Greek philosopher who taught the four elements and the forces of love and strife. Among the philosophers of Limbo.
The Greek philosopher famed for the doctrine of constant flux ('all things flow'). Seen in Limbo.
The ancient Greek physician and botanist who 'gathered the powers of things' (the properties of plants). Named among the wise in Limbo.
The legendary Greek poet and musician whose song could move stones and beasts. Seen among the honored souls of Limbo.
Marcus Tullius Cicero, the great Roman orator and writer (106–43 BC). Named (as 'Tully') among the wise in Limbo.
The Roman historian (59 BC–17 AD), author of a monumental history of Rome. Among the honored souls of Limbo.
The Roman Stoic philosopher and dramatist (c. 4 BC–65 AD), here 'the moralist Seneca.' Seen in Limbo.
The ancient Greek mathematician, founder of geometry. Named 'Euclid the geometer' among the wise of Limbo.
The Greco-Egyptian astronomer (2nd century AD) whose earth-centered model of the heavens dominated the Middle Ages. Seen in Limbo.
The great ancient Greek physician (c. 129–216 AD) whose medical writings ruled medieval medicine. Among the wise of Limbo.
The ancient Greek physician (c. 460–370 BC), the 'father of medicine.' Seen among the wise in Limbo.
The Persian philosopher and physician Ibn Sina (980–1037), hugely influential in medieval Europe. Among the wise souls of Limbo.
The Muslim philosopher Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), called 'who wrote the great Commentary' for his celebrated commentaries on Aristotle. Seen in Limbo.
The monstrous judge of Hell who assigns each damned soul its circle by coiling his tail. In life a king of Crete; here he 'weighs the sins of each.'
The legendary queen of Assyria, infamous for lust, who 'made desire lawful in her code.' The first of the lustful souls Virgil points out.
The legendary king of Assyria, husband (and in some accounts son) of Semiramis. She is said to have 'followed Ninus.'
The Muslim ruler of Dante's own day, said now to hold the land Semiramis once governed (Babylon / the East).
The queen of Carthage who killed herself for love of Aeneas after he abandoned her, breaking faith with the memory of her dead husband Sychaeus. Identified as 'the one who killed herself for love.'
The murdered first husband of Dido; her vow of faithfulness to his ashes is the 'faith' she broke by loving Aeneas.
The queen of Egypt (69–30 BC), lover of Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, 'who lived for pleasure.' Among the lustful souls.
Helen of Troy, whose abduction sparked the Trojan War, 'for whom so many cruel years wheeled round.' Among the lustful.
The greatest Greek warrior of the Trojan War, who in medieval legend was lured to his death by love of Polyxena ('fought with Love at the very end'). Among the lustful souls.
The Trojan prince whose love for Helen began the Trojan War. Among the souls 'Love had cut away from our life.'
The knight of medieval romance whose forbidden love for Iseult led to his death. Named among the lustful.

Francesca da Rimini, a noblewoman of Dante's century, murdered with her lover Paolo (her husband's brother) when their affair was discovered. She tells Dante their love grew from reading of Lancelot. The most famous of the lustful souls.
The great river of northern Italy. Francesca names the city on its shore (Ravenna) as her birthplace.

The first ring of the lowest circle of Hell, named for Cain, reserved for those who betray their kin. Francesca says it 'waits for the one who put out our lives' — her husband, who murdered her and Paolo.
The knight of Arthurian romance whose adulterous love for Queen Guinevere Francesca and Paolo were reading about when their own passion overcame them.

Gallehault, the go-between who arranged the first kiss of Lancelot and Guinevere; Francesca says the book itself, and its author, were a 'Galeotto' (a pander) to her and Paolo. The name became a byword for a seductive go-between.
The monstrous three-throated dog of classical myth who guards the gluttons in the third circle, barking, clawing, and flaying the souls sunk in the freezing muck.
A Florentine glutton, the first soul from Dante's own city he meets in Hell. He prophesies the bloody factional strife to come in Florence.
Florence, torn by the feud of the Black and White Guelphs. Ciacco foretells its civil bloodshed and the rise and fall of its factions.
The White Guelphs of Florence, led by the Cerchi family who came from the rural Val di Sieve. Ciacco foretells they will first drive out the rival party.

Farinata degli Uberti, the great Ghibelline leader of Florence (d. 1264), who almost destroyed the city but alone defended it from being razed. He rises heretical and proud from his burning tomb in the sixth circle.
Tegghiaio Aldobrandi, a respected Florentine of an earlier generation whom Dante asks about. Found among the sinners lower in Hell.
A worthy Florentine of the past Dante inquires after; he later appears among the sodomites in the lower circles.
A Florentine Dante names among the worthy men of the past whose fate he wishes to learn. He does not reappear.
Mosca dei Lamberti, a Florentine whose violent counsel helped spark the city's factional feuds; Dante asks after him and later finds him among the sowers of discord.
The bloated, snarling guardian of the fourth circle, where the greedy and wasteful are punished. A figure of wealth, he collapses at Virgil's rebuke.
The archangel who led the loyal angels against the rebellion of Satan, 'taking his vengeance on the proud rebellion.' Virgil invokes him to subdue Plutus.
The opening cry of Plutus, 'Pape Satàn, pape Satàn aleppe,' a famous untranslatable phrase invoking Satan in his 'strangled, clucking voice.'
The deadly whirlwind-whirlpool of classical myth (off Sicily), used to picture how the hoarders and wasters crash and rebound against each other.

The divine 'minister' or angelic power Virgil describes, appointed by God to shift wealth from people to people. Far from blind chance, she carries out God's hidden plan and rejoices in her work, deaf to the curses of mankind.
The marsh-like fifth river of Hell, made by the dark stream that drains down through the lower circles. In its mire the wrathful tear at one another and the sullen lie gurgling beneath the surface.
The wrathful ferryman who pilots the boat across the Styx, raging at his passengers. In myth a king who burned Apollo's temple.
An arrogant Florentine, 'that raging Florentine spirit,' who lunges at Dante's boat in the Styx and is torn apart by the other wrathful souls to Dante's grim satisfaction.
The walled lower city of Hell, glowing red with its eternal inner fire, holding the worse sinners. (Dis is also a classical name for the underworld god / Satan, who 'sits enthroned' at its center.)
A pitiless sorceress of classical legend who could call the dead back into their bodies. Virgil says she once conjured him down into the lowest pit of Hell.
The lowest, darkest pit of Hell (Judecca, named for Judas the betrayer of Christ), 'the farthest from the heaven that turns all things,' where Virgil was once sent to fetch a spirit.
The three vengeful goddesses of Greek myth, snake-haired handmaids of the 'queen of everlasting grief' (Proserpina/Hecate), who guard the walls of Dis and threaten to call up Medusa against Dante.
One of the three Furies, pointed out on the left as they tear at their own breasts and shriek atop the tower of Dis.
One of the three Furies, 'the one weeping on the right,' guarding the city of Dis.
One of the three Furies, standing between Megaera and Alecto on the walls of Dis.
The snake-haired Gorgon of myth whose gaze turned onlookers to stone. The Furies cry for her to come and petrify Dante, so Virgil seals Dante's eyes.
The Greek hero who descended into the underworld to abduct Proserpina and was punished there. The Furies recall they once 'failed to avenge the assault of Theseus.'

A heavenly messenger (an angel, often read as bearing Christ's authority) who crosses the Styx untouched, opens the gates of Dis with a wand, and rebukes the rebel demons. He scorns Hell and departs at once.
A city in Provence (southern France) famous for its ancient Roman tombs (the Alyscamps). Dante compares the field of burning sepulchers in Dis to it.
A town on the Istrian coast near the Quarnaro gulf, likewise known for its old tombs; compared to the field of graves in Dis.
The gulf (Kvarner, on the Adriatic) near Pola 'that closes Italy in and bathes its edges.'
The great river of southern France that 'goes still' near Arles, used in the comparison to the tomb-field of Dis.
The leaders of heretical sects, punished in the sixth circle inside burning tombs. The chief heresy here is denying the soul's immortality.
The valley where, by biblical tradition, the Last Judgment will take place. The buried heretics will return there to reclaim their bodies before their tombs are sealed forever.
The Greek philosopher (341–270 BC) who taught that the soul dies with the body. He and his followers lie in the burning tombs of the heretics.
A native of Tuscany, the region of Florence; Farinata recognizes Dante as a fellow Tuscan by his speech.
Florence, Dante's and Farinata's native city, which Farinata says he was 'perhaps too much a scourge.'
Guido Cavalcanti, the poet and Dante's friend, son of the shade Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti who rises beside Farinata. The grieving father asks why his son is not with Dante.
Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti, the Epicurean father of Dante's friend Guido, who rises 'uncovered to the chin' from his tomb and despairs, thinking his son is dead.
The river near Montaperti where the Ghibellines (Farinata's side) slaughtered the Florentine Guelphs in 1260, staining the water red. The carnage explains Florence's lasting hatred of his line.

glossary.term: the lady who reigns down here
glossary.gloss: Proserpina (Hecate), queen of the underworld, identified with the moon. Farinata measures time by her — within 'fifty months' Dante too will know the pain of exile.
Emperor Frederick II (1194–1250), the brilliant Hohenstaufen ruler reputed an Epicurean and skeptic. He lies among the heretics in the burning tombs.
Cardinal Ottaviano degli Ubaldini, a powerful Ghibelline churchman reputed to disbelieve in the soul, lying among the heretics with Frederick II.
Pope Anastasius II, whom medieval legend (wrongly) accused of heresy, said to have been led astray by the deacon Photinus. His tomb marks the entrance to lower Hell.
The deacon who, by legend, drew Pope Anastasius into heresy ('off the straight way').

The principle, never named but everywhere at work, by which each sinner's punishment mirrors or inverts the sin — the lustful blown by storm, the gluttons in filth, the wrathful tearing at each other. (Virgil's speech here lays out Hell's whole moral architecture.)

Virgil's classification of sin: the violent (against neighbor, self, and God) in the seventh circle, then the fraudulent in the eighth, and the betrayers in the ninth — 'fraud, the vice unique to man,' sinks lowest of all.

In Virgil's Aristotelian scheme, the failure of self-control (lust, gluttony, greed, wrath) punished outside the city of Dis. It offends God less than malice or brute violence, and earns lighter punishment.
The biblical city destroyed for its sins; here a byword for the 'violence against nature' punished in the seventh circle ('Sodom and Cahors').
A French city notorious in the Middle Ages for usury; named with Sodom as the home of those who do violence against God and nature.
Lending money at interest, which Virgil explains is a sin against Nature and God's design, since the usurer makes money breed money instead of living by honest labor or craft.
The constellation Pisces, rising at the horizon. Virgil reads it as a clock to mark the hour before dawn.
The constellation of the Great Bear / Big Dipper (the 'Wain' or wagon), used with the wind Caurus to tell the time and direction.
The northwest wind of classical naming; Virgil locates the Wain over it to fix the hour and the compass.
The Mediterranean island, home of King Minos and his monstrous stepson the Minotaur, called 'the shame of Crete.'

The Minotaur, the half-man, half-bull monster conceived when Pasiphaë (Minos's wife) mated with a bull while hidden in a wooden ('counterfeit') cow. It guards the entrance to the circle of the violent.
Theseus, who slew the Minotaur. Virgil taunts the beast by recalling 'the man who killed you up in the world above.'

The bull-headed monster of Crete, born of Pasiphaë and a bull, slain by Theseus with the help of Ariadne's thread. It rages at the lip of the seventh circle and Dante and Virgil slip past while it reels.

glossary.term: the one's sister and her thread
glossary.gloss: Ariadne, sister (half-sister) of the Minotaur, who gave Theseus the thread to escape the labyrinth after killing the beast. Virgil mocks the Minotaur with the memory.

glossary.term: He who carried off the great spoils
glossary.gloss: Christ, who at the Harrowing of Hell descended into Dis and led away the saved souls ('the great spoils of the highest circle'). The earthquake at his death shattered the cliff here.
aliases: He came who carried off from Dis

glossary.gloss: The half-man, half-horse creatures of Greek myth, here armed with bows, who patrol the river of boiling blood and shoot any soul that rises above its allotted depth.
The wisest of the Centaurs, who in myth raised the hero Achilles. He leads the Centaur troop guarding the river of blood and assigns Nessus to ferry Dante across.
A Centaur who died for love of Deianira and avenged himself even in death (his poisoned blood later killed Hercules). Chiron sends him to guide Dante along the river of blood.
The wife of Hercules, for whom the Centaur Nessus died; his dying trick later brought about Hercules's death. Named as the cause of Nessus's death.
A Centaur 'so full of rage,' one of the three who confront Dante and Virgil at the river of blood.
Phlegethon, the boiling-red river in the first round of the seventh circle, in which the violent against others (tyrants and murderers) are immersed to the depth their guilt deserves.
Likely Alexander the Great (or a tyrant of Pherae), named among the bloody tyrants sunk in the boiling river for their merciless violence.
Dionysius the tyrant of Syracuse, infamous for cruelty, 'who gave Sicily its years of grief.' Among the violent tyrants in the river of blood.
Ezzelino da Romano (1194–1259), the savage Ghibelline tyrant of northern Italy, recognized by 'the hair so black.' Sunk among the bloody tyrants.
Obizzo II d'Este, marquis of Ferrara, a cruel lord said to have been murdered by his own stepson. The fair-haired tyrant beside Ezzelino in the river of blood.

Guy de Montfort, who murdered Prince Henry of England in a church ('split open, in the very lap of God, the heart that is still honored on the Thames'). His victim's heart was kept in a relic in London.
Attila the Hun (d. 453), 'a scourge on the earth,' the conqueror whose savagery places him among the violent tyrants on the far side of the boiling river.
A bloody warrior-king (Pyrrhus of Epirus, or Achilles's son), named among the tyrants steeped deepest in the river of blood.
A violent figure (Sextus Pompey, the pirate son of Pompey, or Tarquin's son) named among the tyrants in the boiling blood.
A notorious highway robber of Dante's day, drawing his tears from the boiling blood for the violence he did 'on the open roads.'
A Tuscan nobleman turned brigand, infamous for plunder on the highways. Punished with Rinier da Corneto in the river of blood.
Dante's home city, the constant background of these cantos — its bloody factional strife (Black and White Guelphs), its banishment of Dante, and the deeds of its great men recur throughout.
A disembodied soul of the dead, the form in which the damned appear. Their bodies look real but are weightless; Dante, being alive, casts a shadow and moves what he touches.
'A second death' is the cry of the damned — the wish to be annihilated, denied to them since their punishment is eternal. It marks the hopelessness that defines Hell.
Monstrous creatures with women's faces and the bodies of birds with clawed feet. They nest in the thorn-trees of the Wood of the Suicides and feed on the leaves, causing the trapped souls fresh pain.
The people of Troy. In legend, the Harpies harassed the wandering Trojans (led by Aeneas) and foretold their coming hardships.
Islands in the Ionian Sea where, in Virgil's Aeneid, the Harpies attacked the Trojans and prophesied their suffering.
A river in Tuscany; together with Corneto it marks the wild, untamed coastal region (the Maremma) that Dante compares to this savage wood.
A town on the Tuscan coast; with the river Cecina it bounds the wild Maremma district full of thickets and beasts.
A primitive variety of wheat. The suicide's soul, once fallen into the wood, sprouts and grows like a grain of spelt into a thorn-tree.
Frederick II, the Holy Roman Emperor (1194-1250). The speaking soul, Pier della Vigna, was his trusted chancellor who 'held both keys' to the emperor's heart.
Not named directly here but the speaker: Frederick II's loyal minister, who, falsely accused of treason and imprisoned, killed himself out of despair. He pleads that he was always faithful.

A profligate Sienese (Lano da Siena) who squandered his fortune and is now one of the two souls torn apart by hounds in the wood for wasting his goods. The taunt recalls his death at the battle by the Toppo.
The site of a battle (Pieve al Toppo, 1288) where the Sienese were ambushed and Lano was killed; the speaker mocks how slow Lano's legs are now compared to that day.
A notorious Paduan spendthrift who wasted his wealth recklessly. Here he is one of the squanderers hunted and torn by the black hounds in the wood.
John the Baptist, whose image appeared on Florence's coins. Florence traded its first patron, the pagan god Mars, for the Baptist; the abandoned Mars is said to keep the city torn by strife.
The river running through Florence. A fragment of the old statue of Mars stood by the bridge over the Arno; the soul says only that relic keeps the rebuilt city from being doomed.
Cato the Younger, the Roman statesman who, in legend, led an army across the burning Libyan desert. Dante compares the scorched sand of this ring to that wasteland Cato crossed.
Jupiter, king of the Roman gods. Capaneus defiantly dares Jove to keep hurling thunderbolts at him, the way Jove struck him down at Thebes.
The Roman god of fire and the forge, Jove's blacksmith. He and his helpers forge the thunderbolts; Capaneus scornfully invokes the cry for his help at the war of the giants.
The Sicilian name for Mount Etna, believed to house Vulcan's forge under the volcano where the thunderbolts are made.
The battlefield where the giants warred against the gods and Jove struck them down with thunderbolts forged by Vulcan; Capaneus recalls it in his defiance.

One of the Seven Kings who besieged Thebes; he blasphemed and defied the gods and was killed by a thunderbolt from Jove. Here he lies under the rain of fire, still raging and scornful, his pride his greatest torment.
The seven champions who led the doomed assault on the city of Thebes (the 'Seven Against Thebes'). Capaneus was one of them.
aliases: Seven Kings who laid siege to Thebes

glossary.gloss: The ancient Greek city besieged by the Seven Kings; Capaneus blasphemed before its walls and was killed there.
A hot sulfur spring near Viterbo whose red water was channeled to a district of prostitutes. Dante compares the blood-red stream crossing the sand to that brook.
The mountain on Crete, once lush, where the infant Jupiter was hidden from his father Saturn. Inside it now stands the great statue, the Old Man of Crete.
In myth, the mother of Jupiter, who hid her infant son on Mount Ida and had loud noises raised to drown out his cries so his father Saturn would not find and devour him.
A city in Egypt; the Old Man of Crete turns his back toward it (the decadent East) and gazes toward Rome (the ideal).
The river of boiling blood in Hell, formed from the tears of the Old Man of Crete. Virgil reveals that the red stream they see is in fact Phlegethon.
The frozen lake at the very bottom of Hell, formed from the tears of the Old Man of Crete; the lowest point, where there is no further descent.
The river of forgetfulness, located not in Hell but in the Earthly Paradise atop Mount Purgatory, where cleansed souls wash away the memory of their sins.

A giant statue inside Mount Ida, made of gold, silver, brass, iron, and a clay foot, cracked and weeping. Its tears form Hell's four rivers; it symbolizes the decline of human history through the ages.
The people of Flanders, who build dikes between Cadsand and Bruges to hold back the sea. Dante compares the stone embankments of this ring to their flood-walls.
A city in Flanders; with Cadsand it marks the coastal stretch where the Flemings raise sea-walls, the image Dante uses for these banks.
A place on the Flemish coast; with Bruges it bounds the region where the Flemings build dikes against the sea.
The people of Padua, who build embankments along the river Brenta to protect their towns from spring floods. Dante compares the stone banks here to their works.
A river near Padua, prone to flooding when the snow melts; the Paduans wall it in, an image for these embankments.
A mountainous Alpine region whose thaw swells the river Brenta, forcing the Paduans to build their flood-walls.

A revered Florentine scholar, statesman, and writer who was Dante's mentor in his youth. Dante finds him among the sodomites running under the rain of fire and addresses him with deep affection and respect.
The ancient hill-town above Florence. Brunetto blames Florence's worst citizens on descent from Fiesole, calling them coarse and grasping, and warns Dante they will turn on him.
Bitter, sour fruit trees. Brunetto uses them as an image for the harsh Florentines among whom a noble man (the 'sweet fig') cannot flourish.
A famous ancient grammarian. Brunetto names him among the learned men punished here for the 'one same sin' of sodomy.
A renowned 13th-century Florentine jurist and law professor; Brunetto names him among the scholars suffering here.
A title of the Pope ('Servant of the Servants of God'). Brunetto refers obliquely to the pope (Boniface VIII) who transferred a sinful bishop from Florence (the Arno) to Vicenza (the Bacchiglione).
The river of Vicenza; Brunetto says the disgraced cleric was moved by the pope from the Arno (Florence) to the Bacchiglione (Vicenza), where he died.
Brunetto's great encyclopedic work, the Tresor (Li Livres dou Tresor). He commends it to Dante as the book in which he still lives on.
aliases: Treasure, the book I still live in

glossary.gloss: The city that held an annual footrace for a prize of green cloth. Brunetto, departing, is compared to the runner who wins, not loses, that race.
The prize banner of green fabric awarded to the winner of Verona's annual footrace; Brunetto running off is likened to its winner.
A famously virtuous Florentine noblewoman; Guido Guerra is identified as her grandson, marking his good lineage.
A distinguished Florentine nobleman and military leader of Dante's party, grandson of the good Gualdrada. Dante meets him among the sodomites and honors his deeds.
A respected Florentine knight whose counsel (against a disastrous battle) went unheeded. Dante meets him among the sodomites and laments his fate.
A Florentine courtier recently dead, whose news of the city's decline torments the three souls. Dante uses him to set up his lament over Florence's corruption.
A peak in the western Alps, source of the river (the Montone/Acquacheta) whose great waterfall Dante compares to the cascade plunging into the next circle.
The mountain range running down Italy. Dante traces the river's course down their slopes to set up the simile of the great waterfall.
The upper name of a river (later the Montone) that plunges in a single great leap near the monastery of San Benedetto; Dante compares the waterfall into the next circle to it.
A town in the Romagna where the river Acquacheta changes its name to the Montone; used in the waterfall simile.
A mountain monastery (San Benedetto in Alpe) near which the Acquacheta river crashes down in a single great leap; part of the waterfall comparison.
The spotted beast that blocked Dante's path at the poem's opening, traditionally read as a symbol of fraud or lust. Dante mentions the cord he had thought to catch it with.
The belt Dante wears, which he unwinds and hands to Virgil. Virgil flings it into the abyss as a signal, summoning the monster Geryon up from the deep.
The monster who embodies fraud: an honest, kindly human face on a serpent's body with hairy paws and a scorpion's stinging tail. He carries Dante and Virgil down on his back into the eighth circle.
In myth, a mortal weaver turned into a spider for challenging the goddess Minerva. The bright patterns on Geryon's hide are said to surpass even her famous webs.
Used for the rich woven cloths of the East; no Turk or Tartar ever made fabric as colorful as Geryon's painted hide.
The Mongols/Central Asians, famed for richly colored woven cloth; Geryon's hide is said to outdo theirs.
A Paduan usurer not yet dead; one of the seated usurers foretells that Vitaliano will join him here in the future, at his left side.
Sinners punished for graft and corruption in public office (selling justice, favors, or appointments for money). They are boiled in pitch in the fifth ditch and guarded by the Malebranche demons.
Those who lent money at interest, condemned as violent against God's art (honest labor). They sit on the burning sand, each with a money-pouch bearing his family crest hung from his neck.
In myth, the youth who lost control of the sun-chariot of his father Helios and scorched the sky, leaving the scar of the Milky Way. Dante recalls his terror to convey his own fear riding Geryon.
In myth, the boy whose wax wings melted when he flew too near the sun, sending him plunging into the sea while his father Daedalus cried out. Dante recalls his fall to convey his fear on Geryon.
The name of the eighth circle of Hell ('Evil Pockets'), a great iron-gray funnel divided into ten concentric stone ditches, each holding a different kind of fraud.
The Holy Year of 1300, when huge crowds of pilgrims came to Rome; the Romans devised a two-way traffic system on the bridge over the Tiber, which Dante compares to the marching sinners.
The great basilica in Rome, a goal of the Jubilee pilgrims; one stream of the crowd walked toward it across the bridge, in Dante's traffic simile.
A hill in Rome (Monte Giordano) toward which the other stream of Jubilee pilgrims walked across the bridge, in Dante's crowd simile.
A Bolognese politician among the panders and seducers, whipped by demons. He confesses he sold his own sister Ghisolabella to a marquis.
The beautiful sister of Venedico Caccianemico, whom he handed over to satisfy the lust of a marquis; his act of pandering damns him.
The Marquis of Este (Obizzo II), to whom Venedico delivered his sister Ghisolabella.
The people of Bologna. Venedico notes that the ditch of panders is crammed with his fellow Bolognese; later the Jovial Friars are also Bolognese.
A dialect word for 'yes' used between the rivers Reno and Savena, i.e. in Bologna's territory; Venedico uses it to mark how many Bolognese are damned here.
A river marking the territory of Bologna; with the Savena it bounds the area where the dialect 'sipa' is spoken.
A river marking the territory of Bologna; with the Reno it bounds the region where 'sipa' is said.
The Greek hero who led the Argonauts to win the Golden Fleece (the Ram) from Colchis. Punished here as a seducer for abandoning Hypsipyle and Medea, he still carries a kingly look.
The people of Colchis, from whom Jason and the Argonauts seized the Golden Fleece (the Ram) by guile.
The Golden Fleece, the prize Jason took from the Colchians; named for the golden ram whose hide it was.
The island where the women had murdered all their men; Jason stopped there and seduced and abandoned the young Hypsipyle.
The young woman of Lemnos who saved her own father from the island's massacre, only to be seduced, made pregnant, and abandoned by Jason.
The Colchian princess who helped Jason win the Fleece and whom he later betrayed; her abandonment is among the wrongs for which Jason is punished here.
A flatterer from Lucca, found sunk in filth in the ditch of the flatterers. He admits his fawning, insatiable tongue dragged him down here.
A Tuscan city; home of Alessio Interminei the flatterer, and later condemned by the demons as a town full of barrators.
A courtesan from a Roman comedy, used here as the type of the flatterer. She is shown filthy and scratching, the whore who answered her lover's question with extravagant praise.

The sorcerer in the Book of Acts who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit with money. From him comes the word 'simony,' and his followers (corrupt clergy who sold sacred offices) are punished here.
The sin of buying or selling sacred offices, sacraments, or church positions for money, named after Simon Magus. Its practitioners are stuffed head-down in burning holes in this ditch.
The Baptistery of San Giovanni in Florence, where Dante was baptized; he compares the round holes the simonists are stuck in to its baptismal fonts.
Pope Boniface VIII. The buried simonist (Pope Nicholas III) mistakes Dante for Boniface, whom he expects to arrive after his own death and take his place in the burning hole.
The heraldic emblem of the Orsini family ('orsa' means she-bear). The damned pope calls himself a 'son of the She-bear,' i.e. an Orsini (Nicholas III), who enriched his kin.
The children/kinsmen of the Orsini pope ('son of the She-bear'); he confesses he was so eager to advance his 'cubs' that he pocketed wealth and damned himself.
A pope (the 'shepherd' of the Church). The buried pope foretells a still worse 'lawless Shepherd' to come from the west (Pope Clement V).
A book of the Bible telling of a corrupt high priest, Jason, who bought his office. The damned pope compares the coming Clement V to that biblical Jason.
Philip IV of France, who would bend the future pope (Clement V) to his will, as the biblical king bent to the high priest Jason.
The apostle chosen by lot to replace Judas after the betrayal. Dante notes that no money changed hands in his selection, unlike the simonists' dealings.
Charles of Anjou, the king the simonist pope (Nicholas III) plotted against; Dante taunts him about the ill-gotten money that emboldened him.
Saint John, author of Revelation, who saw the vision of the great whore seated on the waters. Dante applies that vision of corruption to the simonist popes.
The Roman emperor whose supposed 'Donation' gave wealth and lands to the Church. Dante laments that this dowry, not Constantine's conversion, was the mother of the Church's corruption.
One of the Seven Kings against Thebes, a seer who foresaw his own death and was swallowed by the earth in mid-battle. He is among the diviners here, his head twisted backward.

The famous blind prophet of Thebes who was once changed into a woman for seven years, then back into a man after striking two coupling serpents again. He walks here with his head twisted backward among the soothsayers.
An Etruscan soothsayer who lived in a cave among the white marble hills of Luni and read the future in the stars; he is punished here among the diviners.
A region in the marble hills of Liguria (near Carrara) where the soothsayer Aruns made his cave-home with clear views of the stars and sea.
The people of Carrara, who work the white marble below the hills of Luni where Aruns lived.
A prophetess, daughter of Tiresias, who wandered the world after Thebes fell and finally settled on the marshy site where the city of Mantua (Virgil's birthplace) was later founded.
The god associated with Thebes ('the city of Bacchus'); when Thebes was enslaved, Manto fled it and wandered the world.
The old name for Lake Garda in northern Italy, at the foot of the Alps near the Tyrol; Virgil traces its waters in describing how Mantua came to be founded.
A town on Lake Benaco (Lake Garda); with Val Camonica it bounds the region whose springs feed the lake.
An Alpine valley; with Garda it marks the area whose thousand springs flow down to feed Lake Benaco.
A fortified town at the southern end of Lake Garda where its waters spill out; a stronghold facing Brescia and Bergamo.
The river that flows out of Lake Garda; once it starts running it is no longer called Benaco but the Mincio, and it passes near Mantua.
Virgil's birthplace, founded on the marshy land where the prophetess Manto had died. Virgil insists this is the true story of how his native city got its name.
A ruling family of Mantua whose foolishness, exploited by Pinamonte's treachery, led to the city being emptied of much of its population.
A scheming Mantuan (Pinamonte dei Bonacolsi) who tricked the gullible Casalodi and drove out the nobility, depopulating the city.
A diviner who foretold the future by reading signs (such as the flight of birds). Several of the damned here, like Eurypylus and Calchas, were augurs.
The Greek seer who, with Eurypylus, fixed the lucky moment for the Greek fleet to sail from Aulis to Troy. Referenced among the soothsayers.
The Greek port where the fleet gathered before sailing to Troy; there the augurs Calchas and Eurypylus chose the moment to cut the cables.
A Greek augur who, with Calchas, set the time for the fleet to leave Aulis for Troy. Virgil says his own poem (the Aeneid) sings of him; here he is among the diviners.
A 13th-century scholar at the court of Frederick II famed for astrology and magic. He is among the diviners, recognized by his lean flanks.
A noted 13th-century astrologer from Forlì; named among the soothsayers and fortune-tellers punished in this ditch.
A cobbler of Parma turned fortune-teller, who now wishes (too late) he had stuck to his shoemaking; punished among the diviners.
The biblical first murderer, whom medieval folklore placed in the moon carrying a bundle of thorns (the 'man in the moon'). Virgil uses 'Cain and his thorns' to tell the time by the setting moon.
aliases: Cain and his bundle of thorns

glossary.gloss: A city in Spain near the western edge of the known world; Virgil uses the moon's position over the sea near Seville to mark the hour.
The squad of winged, hook-wielding demons ('Evil Claws') who guard the boiling pitch of the barrators in the fifth ditch. They torment the sinners and menace Dante and Virgil.
The patron saint of the city of Lucca; an 'Elder of Saint Zita' simply means a magistrate of Lucca, one of whom is dumped into the pitch as a barrator.
A Lucchese politician sarcastically named as the one supposedly honest man in Lucca ('every man there is a barrator but Bonturo') — in fact he was the most corrupt of all.
A revered ancient crucifix in Lucca (the 'Volto Santo'). The demons jeer that 'no Holy Face does any good down here' as the barrator surfaces face-up in the pitch.
A river near Lucca where people went swimming; the demons taunt the boiling barrator that this is not how he used to swim back in the Serchio.
The great shipyard of Venice, where workers boiled sticky pitch all winter to caulk ships. Dante compares the boiling pitch of this ditch to that scene.
The chief of the Malebranche demons ('Evil Tail'). He deceitfully tells Virgil there is a path ahead and lies that the next bridge is intact, sending an escort that nearly traps the travelers.
One of the Malebranche demons; Malacoda restrains him ('Easy, Scarmiglione') when he moves to hook Dante.
A castle near Pisa whose garrison surrendered under safe-conduct in 1289 (a battle Dante witnessed) and marched out fearfully through enemy ranks; Dante recalls their terror as his own.
One of the ten Malebranche demons named by Malacoda. Later he rashly tries to chase an escaping barrator and ends up fighting his own comrade.
One of the ten Malebranche demons. After the barrator escapes, he turns on his own comrade Alichino and they both fall into the boiling pitch.
One of the ten Malebranche demons named by Malacoda; he sees through the barrator's trick to leap back into the pitch.
The demon Malacoda puts in charge of the squad of ten Malebranche ('Curly Beard'). He directs the others and serves as their marshal over the boiling pitch.
One of the ten Malebranche demons; he loses patience and tears a tendon loose from the captured barrator's arm.
One of the ten Malebranche demons; he too lunges to claw the captured barrator's legs.
One of the ten Malebranche demons, who has a boar-like tusk jutting from each side of his mouth and rakes the captured barrator with one of them.
One of the ten Malebranche demons ('Dog-Scratcher'); he hooks a slow barrator by his pitch-matted hair and hauls him out of the boil.
One of the ten Malebranche demons; Barbariccia calls him a 'vicious bird' and holds him back from striking the captive.
One of the ten Malebranche demons, called 'crazy'; the others urge him to sink his claws into the barrator and flay him.
A kingdom in northern Spain; the captured barrator in this ditch says he was born there and served King Thibault before turning to graft.
King Thibault (Theobald) of Navarre, in whose household the captured barrator served before taking bribes; sometimes the soul is called Ciampolo.
The unnamed barrator from Navarre who is hooked and questioned by the demons; he cunningly tricks them and leaps back into the pitch, escaping.
A friar of Gallura in Sardinia, named by the Navarrese as a master of fraud who took bribes to let his lord's enemies go free; he is among the barrators.
A district of Sardinia; Friar Gomita served there as a corrupt official before being damned among the barrators.
A Sardinian official from Logodoro named by the Navarrese as another corrupt grafter who keeps Friar Gomita company in the pitch.
A district of Sardinia; the corrupt official Michel Zanche came from there.
The Mediterranean island home of the barrators Friar Gomita and Michel Zanche, whose talk of its affairs never tires.
A Tuscan city whose territory Dante recalls seeing raided and fought over; he addresses 'men of Arezzo' while comparing the demons' strange signal to military bugles.
The Franciscan friars, who traditionally walked single file along the road. Dante and Virgil are compared to them as they walk silently, one behind the other.
The ancient teller of fables. The recent demon-brawl reminds Dante of Aesop's fable of the frog and the mouse, where treachery rebounds on the schemer.
Sinners punished in the sixth ditch, made to walk forever in cloaks gilded outside but lined with crushing lead — beautiful on the surface, unbearable within, mirroring their false show of virtue.
A German city famed for its monks' robes; the gilded, lead-lined cloaks of the hypocrites are cut in the fashion of monks' robes from Cologne.
Here the heavy gilded-and-lead cloak worn by the hypocrites; the souls wonder by what privilege the living travelers walk 'uncovered by the heavy stole.'
Members of a lax military-religious order (the Knights of Saint Mary, nicknamed the 'Jovial Friars' for their easy life). Catalano and Loderingo, both of this order, are punished here as hypocrites.
A Bolognese member of the Jovial Friars; with Loderingo he was chosen to govern Florence jointly but ruled corruptly. He addresses Dante among the hypocrites.
A Bolognese member of the Jovial Friars who, with Catalano, jointly governed Florence and is damned with him among the hypocrites.
A district of Florence destroyed during the misrule of the Jovial Friars Catalano and Loderingo; the ruin there still testifies to their hypocrisy.

The high priest who advised the Pharisees that it was better for one man (Christ) to die for the people. Crucified naked to the ground with three stakes, he is trampled forever by every passing hypocrite.
The Jewish religious authorities whom Caiaphas counseled to put Christ to death; their council is condemned as 'an evil seed.'
Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who is racked in the same crucified posture in this ditch for his part in condemning Christ.
A northern Italian city, home of the Jovial Friars Catalano and Loderingo and famed for its university; Catalano recalls hearing there of the Devil's lies.
A corrupt official who sells public office, justice, or favors for money. Bonturo's town is said to be full of them, where 'for cash a No is turned to Yes.'

A Tuscan city notorious for violence and faction. Dante curses it as worse than its founders (legendary survivors of the defeated army of Catiline), the breeding ground of the blasphemous thief Vanni Fucci.

glossary.term: the one who fell from the walls at Thebes
glossary.gloss: Capaneus, one of the Seven against Thebes, struck down by Jove for his defiance of the gods. Dante recalls him as the only spirit as openly contemptuous of God as Vanni Fucci.
A creature half man, half horse from Greek myth. Here the monstrous Cacus, his back swarming with snakes, serves as a tormentor of the thieves.
A marshy, snake-ridden coastal region of Tuscany, proverbial for its swarms of serpents and its disease.

A fire-breathing monster who, in myth, stole cattle from Hercules and was clubbed to death by him. Dante sets him among the thieves, snake-covered and apart from his centaur brothers because of his theft.
One of the seven hills of Rome, the cave-lair where the monster Cacus hid and made a 'lake of blood' from his victims.
The great hero of Greek myth, famed for his strength. He killed the cattle-thief Cacus with his club; later his 'warning markers' (the Pillars of Hercules) mark the edge of the known world.
A Florentine thief, member of the Donati family. Absent at first, he reappears transformed into a six-footed serpent that fuses with another sinner.
Agnolo Brunelleschi, a Florentine thief who is merged with a serpent into a single grotesque shape before Dante's eyes.
Two soldiers in Lucan's Pharsalia killed by serpents in the Libyan desert — one melting away, the other swelling up. Dante invokes them as lesser marvels than his own.
The founder of Thebes, who in Ovid's Metamorphoses is changed into a serpent. Dante cites him as a one-way transformation, lesser than the two-way exchange he describes.
A nymph who, fleeing the river-god Alpheus, was turned into a spring in Ovid's Metamorphoses. Dante names her as another single transformation he claims to outdo.
A Florentine thief (Buoso degli Abati or Donati) who is transformed from a man into a serpent in the exchange of shapes Dante witnesses.
A Florentine thief of the Galigai family, nicknamed 'the Lame.' He alone of the three companions keeps his human form unchanged.
A Tuscan town whose people Dante says still 'weep' for Francesco de' Cavalcanti (Guercio), the serpent-spirit; his kin took bloody revenge on Gaville for his murder.
A Tuscan town near Florence. Dante says even little Prato, along with others, craves Florence's downfall — a prophecy of coming disaster for the city.
The chariot of fire in which the prophet Elijah was carried up to heaven (2 Kings). Dante compares the flame-wrapped souls of the false counselors to that distant flame.

glossary.term: the one avenged by the bears
glossary.gloss: The prophet Elisha, who saw Elijah taken up in the fiery chariot and whose mockers were later mauled by bears (2 Kings).

Son of Oedipus who fought his brother Polynices for the throne of Thebes; the two killed each other, and even the flame of their shared funeral pyre split in two from their hatred. Dante likens the forked flame of Ulysses and Diomedes to it.
The Greek hero Odysseus, famed for cunning. Punished here among the false counselors for the trick of the Trojan Horse; he tells how he sailed past the world's edge to his death.
A Greek warrior and Ulysses' partner in the deceits at Troy. The two share a single divided flame, paired in punishment as they were in their schemes.
The woman who loved Achilles and bore his son; Ulysses' trickery lured Achilles away to Troy, and she mourns him still even in death.
The sacred image of Pallas Athena that protected Troy. Ulysses and Diomedes stole it, helping doom the city — one of the crimes for which they burn.
The enchantress who held Ulysses for over a year near Gaeta, transforming his men into beasts. In his tale he describes finally breaking away from her.
A coastal town in Italy where, by Ulysses' account, he lingered with Circe — named after a companion of Aeneas, though, as Ulysses notes, before Aeneas gave it that name.
The faithful wife of Ulysses, who waited for him at Ithaca. Even the love he owed her could not hold back his hunger to sail beyond the known world.
The Pillars of Hercules (the Strait of Gibraltar), set up as a boundary no sailor was meant to cross. Ulysses sails past them into the forbidden ocean.
A North African port opposite Gibraltar, the other landmark Ulysses passes as he leaves the Mediterranean for the open Atlantic.
God, named obliquely by Ulysses as the will that finally sank his ship — the divine power he never names directly.

The brazen bull of the tyrant Phalaris of Agrigento, in which victims were roasted alive so their screams sounded like the bull's bellow; its maker, Perillus, was its first victim. Dante likens the muffled voice inside the flame to it.
The northern-Italian dialect of Lombardy; Virgil's parting words to Ulysses' flame were spoken in it, which the next sinner (Guido da Montefeltro) recognizes.
The region of north-central Italy around Ravenna and Forlì, home to the speaker Guido da Montefeltro. Dante surveys its warring tyrant-cities at Guido's request.
A town in the Marches; Guido da Montefeltro describes his homeland as lying in the mountains between Urbino and the source of the Tiber.
The great river that runs through Rome, here named for its mountain source near Guido da Montefeltro's homeland.

A famous soldier-statesman of Romagna who became a Franciscan friar but was lured by Pope Boniface VIII into giving fraudulent counsel. He is the speaker in the flame, damned among the false counselors.
A city of Romagna, ruled by the da Polenta family ('the Eagle of Polenta') whose emblem covers it and nearby Cervia.
The da Polenta family of Ravenna, whose heraldic eagle 'broods over' the city and Cervia. Dante names rulers by their coats of arms in this survey.
A small coastal town near Ravenna, likewise under the rule of the da Polenta 'Eagle.'
The heraldic green lion's paws of the Ordelaffi family, who ruled Forlì — the city that once withstood a long siege and bloodily repulsed the French.
Malatesta da Verrucchio and his son Malatestino, lords of Rimini, called 'old Mastiff and young one' for their savagery; they killed the Ghibelline leader Montagna.
Montagna de' Parcitati, a Ghibelline leader of Rimini foully murdered by the Malatesta 'Mastiffs.'
Two rivers of Romagna marking the territory of Faenza and Imola, ruled by Maghinardo Pagani ('the young Lion of the white den'), who shifted political sides.
Maghinardo Pagani da Susinana, lord of the cities on the Lamone and Santerno, whose blazon was a blue lion on white; Dante mocks his switching of sides.
A river of Romagna; the city on its bank (Cesena) is described as living 'between tyranny and freedom.'
Pope Boniface VIII, the 'Prince of the modern Pharisees,' who dragged Guido da Montefeltro back into sin by demanding cunning advice and granting him false absolution.
The seat of papal power in Rome; Boniface VIII waged his war 'near the Lateran' — against fellow Christians (the Colonna family), not infidels.
The medieval term for Muslims; Dante notes that Boniface's war was not against them but against fellow Christians.
The last Christian stronghold in the Holy Land, lost to the Muslims in 1291. Dante notes Boniface's Christian enemies had not even fought there for the faith.
The Muslim ruler of Egypt; Dante notes Boniface's enemies had not even traded in his forbidden lands — they were no infidels but Christians.
Pope Sylvester I, who in legend cured Constantine's leprosy. The cure is the image for Boniface's seeking out Guido da Montefeltro.
A mountain north of Rome where, in legend, Pope Sylvester hid and was sought out by Constantine.
A fortified town held by the Colonna family; Boniface VIII sought Guido's advice on how to 'level it to the ground,' which he did by treacherous promise.
The keys of Heaven entrusted to the papacy (the power to bind and loose). Boniface boasts he holds both, taunting that his predecessor (the abdicated Celestine V) 'did not prize' them.
Saint Francis of Assisi, founder of the Franciscan order Guido had joined. He comes for Guido's soul at death but is rebuffed by a demon, since Guido's repentance was void.
A fallen angel (a 'cherub' of evil) who claims Guido's soul, defeating Saint Francis with a logician's argument: one cannot will a sin and repent of it at once.

The region of southeastern Italy, soaked in blood by ancient wars (against Rome and the Trojans) and by the campaigns of Robert Guiscard. Dante invokes its slaughters as less than the carnage of the sowers of discord.
The Norman conqueror of southern Italy in the 11th century, whose long, bloody wars Dante invokes among the slaughters of Apulia.
A pass where, by Dante's account, the Apulian barons betrayed King Manfred by failing to hold it, opening the way to his defeat.
The battlefield where Charles of Anjou defeated Conradin in 1268, thanks to a tactic of the old knight Alardo de Valéry, who 'won the field without lifting a weapon.'
Érard (Alardo) de Valéry, the veteran French commander whose strategy won the battle of Tagliacozzo for Charles of Anjou without his fighting.
The founder of Islam, placed by Dante among the sowers of discord and schism, his body split open from chin to groin. Dante (mistakenly, by medieval belief) treats him as a divider of the church.
Ali ibn Abi Talib, Mohammed's son-in-law and a central figure in Islam's first great schism. He walks before Mohammed, his face cleft from forelock to chin.
A split or division within a religious community or church; the chief sin of this ditch, where those who tore apart what was joined are themselves torn apart.
A heretical preacher who led a sect (the Apostolic Brethren) and was besieged in the mountains; Mohammed sends him a warning to stock up on food. He was captured and burned in 1307.
The northern-Italian town whose forces besieged and starved out Fra Dolcino and his followers.
A man of Romagna, a sower of political discord among the lords of the region; mutilated here, throat slit and nose hacked off, he warns of a coming betrayal at sea.
A town in Piedmont marking one end of the lovely Lombard plain that Pier da Medicina recalls, stretching down to Marcabò.
A fortress near the mouth of the Po, marking the far end of the plain Pier da Medicina remembers.
A town on the Adriatic whose 'two best men,' Guido del Cassero and Angiolello da Carignano, will be treacherously drowned at sea by a tyrant.
Guido del Cassero and Angiolello da Carignano, the two leading men of Fano, prophesied to be flung overboard and drowned near La Cattolica through a tyrant's betrayal.
A town on the Adriatic coast near which the two men of Fano are foretold to be drowned by treachery.
The Roman god of the sea, invoked to say that he never witnessed so great a crime on those waters — not even from pirates.
An ancient Greek city; 'the men of Argos' stands for Greek pirates or seafarers, invoked as a measure of seaborne crime.
A headland on the Adriatic known for dangerous winds; the doomed men of Fano will be drowned before they reach it, so they'll have no need to pray against its gales.
The Roman tribune who, by his urging, pushed Julius Caesar to cross the Rubicon and start civil war. His tongue, that gave divisive counsel, is slit through.

A Provençal troubadour-knight who incited the 'Young King' Henry to rebel against his father Henry II of England. As a sower of discord between father and son, he carries his own severed head like a lantern.
Henry the Young King, son of Henry II of England, whom Bertran de Born goaded into rebellion against his father.
The counselor who in the Bible incited Absalom to rebel against his father King David. Bertran de Born compares his own crime of dividing father and son to Ahithophel's.
The son of King David who rebelled against him, egged on by the wicked counsel of Ahithophel — the biblical parallel to Bertran de Born's sin.
Dante's principle that each sinner's punishment mirrors the sin (the contrapasso). Bertran de Born, who split father from son, carries his head split from his body.
A kinsman of Dante's (a cousin of his father), a sower of discord whose violent death went unavenged by his family. Dante glimpses him pointing accusingly and feels pity.

glossary.term: the one who once held Hautefort
glossary.gloss: Bertran de Born, lord of the castle of Hautefort; Dante was so absorbed in him that he failed to notice his own kinsman Geri del Bello.
A malarial valley in Tuscany whose summer fevers were proverbial; Dante invokes its hospitals' suffering to convey the stench and misery of the falsifiers' ditch.

A Greek island struck by plague that killed all its people and animals; in myth Zeus repopulated it by turning ants into men (the Myrmidons). Dante compares the heaped, sick falsifiers to its dying multitude.
The falsifiers of the tenth ditch — those who corrupted truth in substance: alchemists, counterfeiters, impostors, and liars, each struck with a fitting disease.
An alchemist from Arezzo who tricked the gullible Albert of Siena with a promise to teach him to fly; for that and his alchemy he was burned, and is now a scab-covered falsifier.
A foolish, well-connected Sienese who, deceived by Griffolino's promise to teach him flight, had Griffolino burned for failing.
The master craftsman of myth who made wings to fly. Griffolino jokingly promised to make Albert of Siena a 'Daedalus' — to teach him to fly — which led to his being burned.
The people of Siena, Florence's rival; Dante mocks them as the vainest of peoples, naming their spendthrift 'club' as proof.
A Sienese named with biting sarcasm as a model of 'restraint' — actually one of the notorious spendthrift 'Spendthrift Club' of Siena.
A Sienese mockingly credited with 'discovering' the lavish, costly use of cloves — another of the wastrels Dante satirizes.
A Sienese spendthrift who squandered his vineyards and woods in the riotous 'club' Dante names with sarcasm.
Bartolomeo dei Folcacchieri, nicknamed 'Abbagliato' (the dazed one), a member of the Sienese spendthrift club mocked here.
An alchemist and skilled mimic ('a good ape of nature') who falsified metals and was burned; he speaks as a scab-ridden falsifier and is later savaged by Gianni Schicchi.
The medieval art of transmuting base metals into gold; here a form of falsification punished in the last ditch, since alchemists counterfeited nature itself.
Queen of the Roman gods, whose jealous rage at the Theban house (because Jove loved Semele) drove Athamas to madness. Dante invokes her wrath to introduce the raging falsifiers of identity.
A Theban princess loved by Jove and destroyed by Juno's jealousy; her story is the root of Juno's rage against Thebes.
A king driven mad by Juno's wrath, who mistook his wife and sons for a lioness and cubs and killed his son Learchus. Dante invokes his frenzy to match the fury of the impersonators.
The young son of Athamas, snatched up in his father's madness and dashed against a rock.
Queen of fallen Troy who, having seen her children Polyxena and Polydorus dead, went mad with grief and 'barked like a dog.' Dante cites her frenzy alongside Athamas's.
A daughter of Hecuba and Priam, sacrificed after Troy's fall; her death is one of the blows that drove Hecuba mad.
A son of Hecuba whose murdered body she discovered on the shore — the final grief that broke her mind.
A Florentine who impersonated the dead Buoso Donati to dictate a fraudulent will, winning himself a prize mare. A 'falsifier of persons,' he runs rabid through the ditch, savaging Capocchio.
A princess of myth who, disguising herself, committed incest with her own father. Damned as a falsifier of her person, she is the rabid soul biting through the ditch.
A wealthy Florentine after whose death Gianni Schicchi impersonated him to forge a will and steal a prize mare from the estate.
A counterfeiter who, paid by the Conti Guidi of Romena, struck false gold florins debased with dross. Bloated with dropsy and tormented by thirst, he is a falsifier of coin.
A disease of swelling from fluid retention; Master Adam's body is grotesquely bloated by it, his face out of proportion to his belly, while he burns with unquenchable thirst.
A green, well-watered upland region of Tuscany whose cool brooks run down to the Arno; their remembered image torments the thirsty Master Adam.
A castle of the Conti Guidi in the Casentino where Master Adam counterfeited the Florentine florin; he was burned there for it.
The gold coins of Florence, stamped with John the Baptist; Master Adam counterfeited them with three carats of base metal mixed in.
The Conti Guidi of Romena — the lords (Guido and Alessandro and Aghinolfo) who induced Master Adam to counterfeit the florin and whom he longs to see suffer.
A famous spring (at Siena, or near Romena); Master Adam says he would not trade the sight of his guilty patrons in Hell even for its waters, despite his torturing thirst.

glossary.term: the false woman who accused Joseph
glossary.gloss: Potiphar's wife, who in the Bible falsely accused Joseph of assault when he refused her. A falsifier by lying word, she steams with fever beside Master Adam.
The lying Greek who deceived the Trojans into taking the wooden horse inside their walls. A falsifier by word, he trades blows and insults with Master Adam.
The Trojan Horse, the wooden horse by which the Greeks, with Sinon's lie, smuggled soldiers into Troy. Master Adam taunts Sinon with it.
The youth of myth who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool. 'The mirror of Narcissus' is a sneering periphrasis for water — which the thirsty Master Adam would lap up eagerly.
The spear of Achilles (inherited from his father Peleus), said to heal with a second touch the wound it first gave. Dante likens Virgil's tongue, which shamed then comforted him, to it.
The mountain pass where Charlemagne's rearguard was destroyed; Roland blew his horn there too late. Dante invokes it for the terrible blast of the giants' horn (Nimrod's).
The great Frankish emperor whose holy army was ambushed and destroyed at Roncesvalles, his nephew Roland among the dead.
Charlemagne's heroic nephew, who blew his great horn at the disaster of Roncesvalles. Dante says even that horn was less terrible than the giant Nimrod's blast.
The towering giants who rebelled against the gods, set around the rim of the central pit of Hell, visible from the navel up like turrets. They guard the descent to the frozen lake.
A Tuscan fortress town whose round wall is crowned with a ring of towers; Dante compares the giants standing around the pit's rim to its turrets.
The Roman god of war; Dante says Nature was wise to stop making giants, so as to deny Mars such mighty hands for warfare.

glossary.term: the bronze pinecone at Saint Peter's
glossary.gloss: A giant ancient bronze pinecone (the Pigna) in Rome, used as a measure for the vast face of the giant Nimrod.
The people of Frisia, proverbially tall; Dante says three of them standing on each other's shoulders could not reach the giant's hair.
The biblical king who built the Tower of Babel, the 'mad scheme' that left mankind without a common language. He bellows meaningless words and is understood by no one.
The meaningless gibberish bellowed by the giant Nimrod — his confused, language-less cry, fitting punishment for the one who caused the confusion of tongues at Babel.
One of the giants who warred against the Olympian gods; chained for his rebellion, he shakes himself like an earthquake in his rage.
A hundred-handed giant who fought the gods; Dante wishes to see him, but is told he is farther on, bound and even more ferocious of face.
A giant son of Earth, unbound because he took no part in the war on heaven. Strong enough to lift Hercules, he stoops to set Dante and Virgil down on the frozen floor of Hell.
The Roman general Scipio Africanus, who defeated Hannibal at Zama in the valley near Antaeus's old haunt — the victory that made him 'heir to glory.'
The Carthaginian general defeated by Scipio at Zama; his army's rout in that valley is recalled to flatter the giant Antaeus.
The giants, offspring of the Earth (Gaia), who warred on heaven; some believed they would have won had Antaeus joined them.
Two monstrous giants of myth punished by the gods; Virgil warns Antaeus not to fob them off on these lesser brutes but to set them down himself.
An old unit of length (roughly an arm's span); Antaeus stands 'a full five ells' above the pit, not counting his head — a measure of his huge size.
A leaning tower in Bologna; seen from below as clouds pass over, it seems to topple. Dante likens the stooping giant Antaeus to it.
The fallen archangel, once the most beautiful of the angels, now the monstrous emperor of Hell frozen at the center of the earth. The floor he is fixed in 'swallows Lucifer and Judas.'
Judas Iscariot, the apostle who betrayed Christ — the arch-traitor, named with Lucifer as fixed at the very bottom of Hell, chewed in Lucifer's central mouth.
The Muses, invoked for harsh enough verse; they aided Amphion, who raised the walls of Thebes by the music of his lyre.
A musician of myth who built the walls of Thebes by the power of his music, the stones moving to his lyre. Dante invokes the Muses who helped him.
The great central-European river; even its winter ice in Austria was never so thick, Dante says, as the ice of Cocytus.
The Russian river (the ancient Tanais); its frozen current under a frigid sky is another measure for the deeper ice of Cocytus.
Two great mountains; Dante says that even if one of them crashed down on the ice of Cocytus, it would not crack at the edge.
The first zone of frozen Cocytus, named for Cain, where those who betrayed their own kin are punished — like the two brothers locked head to head.
Alberto degli Alberti, father of the two warring brothers (Napoleone and Alessandro) frozen in Caïna for murdering each other over their inheritance in the Bisenzio valley.
A valley and river in Tuscany that belonged to the Alberti family, whose two sons killed each other and lie frozen in Caïna.

glossary.term: the one run through by Arthur's hand
glossary.gloss: Mordred, the treacherous nephew of King Arthur, slain by Arthur's spear so that the sunlight pierced the wound through his body and shadow — a famous kin-traitor.
Vanni dei Cancellieri of Pistoia, who murdered a kinsman; named among the traitors of Caïna.
A Florentine who murdered a young relative for his inheritance; a traitor to kin, frozen in Caïna and famously known to Tuscans.
Alberto Camicione de' Pazzi, who murdered a kinsman; he names himself in Caïna and awaits a worse relative, Carlino, whose betrayal will make him 'look clean.'
Carlino de' Pazzi, a kinsman whose future treachery (betraying a castle) will be so much worse that Camicion expects to seem innocent by comparison.
The 1260 battle where Florence's Guelfs were disastrously defeated, betrayed by Bocca degli Abati, who cut off the standard-bearer's hand. The traitor Dante kicks demands vengeance for it.
The second zone of frozen Cocytus, named for the Trojan Antenor, where those who betrayed their homeland or party are punished.
Bocca degli Abati, the Florentine traitor who at Montaperti cut off the standard-bearer's hand and caused the Guelf rout. Dante kicks his head and forces out his name.
Buoso da Duera, who for French bribe-money let Charles of Anjou's army pass unopposed — a traitor to his Ghibelline party, weeping in the ice over 'French silver.'
Tesauro dei Beccaria, abbot of Vallombrosa, beheaded by the Florentines for treasonous dealings with the Ghibellines; another traitor of Antenora.
A Florentine Ghibelline who betrayed his own party to side with the people; a traitor of Antenora.
The traitor of the Charlemagne legend who betrayed Roland to ambush at Roncesvalles; the archetype of the betrayer of his lord and homeland.
Tebaldello de' Zambrasi, who treacherously opened the gates of Faenza to the enemy while the city slept; a traitor of Antenora.
A Romagna town whose gates Tebaldello treacherously threw open to the enemy by night.
One of the Seven against Thebes who, mortally wounded, gnawed the head of his slayer Menalippus in his rage. Dante compares Ugolino gnawing Ruggieri's skull to him.
The Theban warrior whose severed head Tydeus gnawed in his dying fury — the mythic image for Ugolino's cannibal-like gnawing of Ruggieri.
Count Ugolino della Gherardesca of Pisa, who, betrayed by Archbishop Ruggieri, was locked with his sons in a tower and starved to death. He gnaws his betrayer's skull and tells the tale.
Archbishop Ruggieri degli Ubaldini of Pisa, who treacherously imprisoned Count Ugolino and his sons in the Tower of Hunger and left them to starve. Ugolino eternally gnaws his head.
The Pisan prison tower where Ruggieri locked Ugolino and his children and starved them to death; named for that horror ever after.
The people of Pisa, whose city Ugolino had governed; Ruggieri turned them against him, and Dante curses Pisa for the cruelty done to Ugolino's innocent sons.
Three powerful Pisan Ghibelline families, allies of Archbishop Ruggieri, figured in Ugolino's dream as the lean hounds leading the deadly hunt.
Anselmuccio, the youngest of Ugolino's children imprisoned and starved with him, who asks his staring father what is wrong.
One of Ugolino's children who, on the fourth day of starvation, falls dead at his father's feet crying for help.
The Tuscan city Dante curses as 'shame of all the peoples' for starving Ugolino's innocent children; he wishes the islands would dam the Arno and drown it.

glossary.term: the country where the word for yes is sì
glossary.gloss: Italy, identified by its word for 'yes' (sì) — Dante's name for his homeland.
Two islands off the Tuscan coast; Dante wishes they would move to dam the mouth of the Arno and drown all of Pisa.
Two of Count Ugolino's sons (or grandsons) starved to death with him in the Tower of Hunger; Dante stresses their youth and innocence.
Pisa, called a 'new Thebes' for its monstrous cruelty — Thebes being the byword for impious family slaughter.
Alberigo dei Manfredi, who murdered his own kin at a banquet by a prearranged signal ('the fruit of the bad garden'). A traitor to guests, his soul is in Hell though his body still lives above.
The third zone of frozen Cocytus, named for Ptolemy who murdered his guests; here those who betrayed guests are punished, their souls falling to Hell even before their bodies die.
One of the three Fates, the one who cuts the thread of life. In Ptolomea, traitors' souls plunge to Hell even before Atropos has cut them loose.
A Genoese who treacherously murdered his father-in-law Michel Zanche at a banquet. His soul is already frozen in Ptolomea though his body still eats and sleeps in the world above.
The people of Genoa, whom Dante curses as set against every virtue and full of every vice, for Branca d'Oria's treachery.
Latin for 'The banners of the king of Hell advance' — Virgil's grim parody of a famous hymn, announcing the approach of Lucifer's vast wings.
The apostle who betrayed Christ; he suffers worst of all, head crushed inside Lucifer's central mouth, legs kicking out — the supreme traitor.
Gaius Cassius, co-conspirator in the murder of Julius Caesar; a powerfully built traitor chewed in the third of Lucifer's three mouths.

The fourth and innermost zone of frozen Cocytus, named for Judas, where the worst traitors — those who betrayed their masters and benefactors — lie wholly buried in the ice with Lucifer at the center.
Another name for Lucifer/Satan; Dante measures the hidden passage out of Hell as 'as far from Beelzebub as the limit of his tomb.'

glossary.term: the vile worm that bores through the world
glossary.gloss: Lucifer, fixed at the earth's exact center; Virgil climbs down his shaggy flanks and, passing the center of gravity, reverses direction to begin the ascent out of Hell.

glossary.term: the Man who was born and lived without a sin
glossary.gloss: Jesus Christ, crucified at Jerusalem (under the hemisphere of the dry land), the sinless Man whose death anchors Dante's cosmic geography.
The chief of the Muses, especially of epic poetry; Dante invokes her at the start of Purgatory to lift his song after the horrors of Hell.
The daughters of Pierus, who challenged the Muses to a singing contest, lost, and were turned into magpies. Dante invokes the Muses whose song defeated them.

glossary.term: the fair planet that calls us to love
glossary.gloss: Venus, the morning star, here brightening the eastern dawn over the mountain of Purgatory.
Pisces, the zodiacal constellation rising just before the sun; Venus 'veils' them as escort in the dawn sky over Purgatory.
Four bright stars in the southern sky over the mountain of Purgatory, seen by 'no one since the first people' (Adam and Eve); traditionally taken to symbolize the four cardinal virtues.
The North-African city where Cato took his own life rather than submit to Caesar; Virgil recalls that 'death in Utica' was not bitter to him for the sake of freedom.

glossary.term: a Lady came down from heaven
glossary.gloss: Beatrice (or by extension divine Grace / the Virgin Mary), the heavenly lady whose prayers sent Virgil to rescue Dante; her authority overrides Cato's challenge.
The angel guarding the entrance to Purgatory, called the 'first' of those in Paradise; Cato bids Virgil cleanse Dante's face before he comes before him.
The humble reed that grows in the wet mud at the base of the mountain of Purgatory; Cato bids Virgil gird Dante with one as a sign of humility. When plucked, it miraculously grows back.
The seven terraces of Mount Purgatory, each purging one of the deadly sins; Virgil asks leave for the pair to pass through them.
Greek and Roman god of poetry, prophecy, and the sun. At the opening of Paradiso, Dante prays to him for the inspiration to describe Heaven, a task harder than the rest of the poem.
The mountain in Greece sacred to Apollo and the Muses, source of poetic inspiration. Dante says that until now one of its two peaks sufficed, but for Paradiso he needs both.
A satyr who challenged Apollo to a music contest, lost, and was flayed alive. Dante asks Apollo to breathe through him as forcefully as when the god drew Marsyas from his own skin.
A river god, father of the nymph Daphne who became the laurel tree. "The leaf of Peneus" means the laurel, the crown of poets.
The chief oracle and shrine of Apollo in Greece. "The glad god of Delphi" is Apollo himself.
A town near Delphi associated with Apollo. Dante hopes that future poets, inspired, will pray for the answer that Cyrrha (Apollo) may grant.
A fisherman in Greek myth who, after eating a magic herb, was transformed into a sea-god. Dante compares his own transhumanizing — passing beyond the merely human — to Glaucus's change.
