Roman goddess of wisdom (Greek Athena). Dante invokes her, with Apollo and the Muses, as the divine wind filling the sail of his poetic voyage into Paradise.
The nine goddesses who inspire poetry, music, and the arts. Dante says they "point me to the Bears" — guide his course like the pole stars.
The constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor, near the north celestial pole, used by sailors to steer. Here a metaphor for the Muses guiding Dante's poetic course.
The far land Jason sailed to with the Argonauts to seize the Golden Fleece, yoking fire-breathing bulls to plow a field. Dante says his readers will be more amazed than those heroes were.
The lowest sphere of Dante's Heaven, the first the pilgrims enter. It holds souls who broke their vows; its surface markings prompt a long discussion of cosmology and light.
The sphere of the fixed stars, which holds countless distinct lights. Beatrice cites its varied stars to disprove the idea that the Moon's spots come merely from dense and thin matter.
The highest, outermost heaven — the motionless realm of pure light where God dwells. Beatrice calls it "the heaven of the divine repose," the source of being and motion for all lower spheres.
The "first moved" — the ninth, fastest-turning sphere just below the Empyrean, which imparts motion to all the heavens beneath it. Dante calls it the sphere "that turns with the greatest haste."
Piccarda Donati, a Florentine nun dragged from her convent and forced to marry. She is the first soul Dante meets in Paradise, in the sphere of the Moon, and explains the joy of accepting God's will.
The third person of the Christian Trinity, the divine love that kindles the affections of the blessed. Piccarda says the souls' loves take fire only in its pleasure.
Christ, figured as the spouse of nuns and of the Church. Souls who take the veil pledge themselves to him until death.

Empress Constance of Sicily, said to have been taken from a convent to marry; mother of Frederick II. "The second wind of Swabia" is Emperor Henry VI, and her son Frederick II is "the third and final power."
A German duchy, home of the Hohenstaufen imperial dynasty. "The second wind of Swabia" refers to Emperor Henry VI, husband of Constance.
The "Hail Mary," a Latin prayer to the Virgin. Piccarda sings it as she fades back into the light of her sphere.
The Old Testament prophet who interpreted King Nebuchadnezzar's forgotten dream, calming his murderous rage. Beatrice reads Dante's unspoken doubts as Daniel read the king's mind.
King of Babylon whose forgotten, troubling dream the prophet Daniel both recalled and interpreted, lifting the king's fury.
The highest order of angels, burning closest to God in love. Beatrice says not even the Seraph "most in-Godded" has a seat in any heaven other than the Empyrean.
An Old Testament prophet and judge of Israel. Beatrice names him among the supreme blessed who, like all souls, truly reside in the Empyrean.
The Virgin Mary, mother of Christ. Beatrice notes that not even she has her seat in any heaven other than the highest, the Empyrean.
The archangel who announced Christ's coming to Mary. Holy Church paints him with a human face so human minds can grasp the spiritual.
In the Book of Tobit, a young man whose blind father was healed by the angel Raphael. "The one who gave Tobias back his healthy sight" is the archangel Raphael.
Plato's dialogue (and its title character) which teaches that each soul returns to its own star. Beatrice corrects the literal reading of this doctrine.
A Roman god and the planet nearest the sun, second sphere of Dante's Heaven, home of souls who did good for fame and honor. Justinian appears here.
Saint Lawrence, a deacon martyred by being roasted on a gridiron, who endured it without yielding. Beatrice cites his unbroken will as a model of constancy.
Gaius Mucius Scaevola, the Roman hero who thrust his own right hand into fire to prove Roman resolve. Beatrice names him alongside Lawrence as an example of unshakable will.
In Greek myth, a son who killed his own mother at his father's command to avenge a betrayal. Beatrice cites him as one who did wrong under coercion rather than lose something dear.
God, the first and supreme source of love. Dante addresses Beatrice as a divine one filled by the love of the First Lover.

glossary.term: the white key and the gold
glossary.gloss: The two keys of the Church's authority — the white key of priestly discernment and the gold key of the power to absolve. Vows may be altered only with both keys' sanction.
An Old Testament judge who rashly vowed to sacrifice whatever met him on his return — and so killed his own daughter. Beatrice cites him as a warning against keeping a sinful vow.

glossary.term: the great leader of the Greeks
glossary.gloss: Agamemnon, commander of the Greek army at Troy, who sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to gain favorable winds. Dante calls his vow as foolish as Jephthah's.
Daughter of Agamemnon, sacrificed by him to secure winds for the voyage to Troy. Her grief and beauty made wise and simple alike weep at such a vow.
The sphere of Mercury, the second heaven, which Dante and Beatrice enter in Canto V. It holds souls who did good chiefly to win earthly fame and honor.

glossary.term: the ancient who took Lavinia for his bride
glossary.gloss: Aeneas, the Trojan founder of the Roman line, who married Lavinia in Italy. He had carried the eagle westward, the direction Constantine later reversed.
The standard and symbol of the Roman Empire, "the bird of God," whose flight Justinian traces through Roman history. To Dante it represents God-ordained universal authority.
The Byzantine emperor ("Caesar I was, and am Justinian") who codified Roman law. He speaks all of Canto VI from the sphere of Mercury, narrating the history of the empire.
Pope Agapetus I, who corrected Justinian's heretical belief that Christ had only one (divine) nature, leading him to true faith before his great work of lawmaking.
Justinian's great general, to whom the emperor entrusted his armies — a sign, Justinian felt, that he himself should focus on law rather than war.
The young son of King Evander, killed fighting alongside Aeneas. Justinian says Roman sovereignty began "from the hour when Pallas died."
Alba Longa, the ancient Latin city where the Roman line dwelt for three centuries before Rome itself, until the duel of three Roman against three Alban champions decided supremacy.
The women seized by Rome's first men to provide wives, an early episode of Roman expansion under the kings.
The Gaulish chieftain who sacked Rome around 390 BC. Justinian lists him among the foes the Roman eagle overcame.
Titus Manlius Torquatus, a stern Roman commander, named among the heroes who won glory under the eagle.
Cincinnatus, the Roman called from his plow to lead Rome, nicknamed for his unkempt hair. Justinian honors him among Rome's great men.
A Roman family famous for self-sacrifice in battle, devoting their lives for victory. Justinian names them among the eagle's heroes.
A celebrated Roman clan of soldiers and statesmen, listed among those who won fame under the imperial eagle.
Pompey the Great, a Roman general who, like Scipio, won early triumphs under the eagle before falling to Caesar.
The river Julius Caesar famously crossed to march on Rome, beginning civil war. Justinian marks it as the launch of Caesar's astonishing campaigns.
The battle in Greece where Caesar decisively defeated Pompey. Justinian says the blow was felt as far as "the warm Nile," where Pompey fled.
A North African king allied with Pompey's faction, defeated when the eagle "came down like lightning" on him.
The chief assassins of Julius Caesar. Justinian notes that for opposing the eagle's rightful bearer they "howl in Hell together" — they are punished in the lowest pit.
A Roman temple whose doors were shut only in times of total peace. Under Augustus the eagle brought such deep peace that it was closed.
The emperor Tiberius, under whom — Justinian says — the eagle achieved its greatest deed: in his reign Christ was crucified, so divine justice "avenged its own wrath" against original sin.
The Roman emperor who destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70. Justinian says he, bearing the eagle, took "vengeance on the vengeance for the ancient sin" — punishing the Jews for the Crucifixion.
A Germanic people who invaded Italy and threatened the Church, until Charlemagne came to her rescue under the eagle's wings.
The fleur-de-lis, emblem of the French royal house and the Guelf party. Justinian condemns those who set this party banner against the universal imperial standard.
The medieval Italian faction supporting the Holy Roman Emperor against the Pope. Justinian rebukes them for misusing the imperial eagle for their own party ends.
The medieval Italian faction siding with the Pope against the Emperor, opposed to the Ghibellines. "This new Charles" and his Guelfs are warned not to drag down the eagle.
Charles II of Naples (or his line), an Angevin Guelf leader whom Justinian warns against opposing the imperial standard, lest he face the talons that mauled greater foes.

Romeo of Villeneuve, a humble pilgrim and able minister who served Raymond Berenger, marrying off his four daughters as queens, only to be slandered and to leave poor. Justinian holds him up as a wronged just man.
Raymond Berenger IV, Count of Provence, whose four daughters all became queens through the management of his loyal minister Romeo, whom he later wronged.
The people of Provence whose slanders against the faithful minister Romeo turned his lord against him. Justinian says their treachery did them no lasting good.
A Latin hymn of praise, "Hosanna, holy God of Hosts," sung by the blessed soul (Justinian) as he and the other spirits return to their dance.
Christ, the second person of the Trinity, who "descended" to join human nature to himself and redeem fallen mankind. Beatrice explains the logic of the Incarnation.

glossary.term: the man who never was born
glossary.gloss: Adam, the first man, who was created rather than born of parents. By refusing God's curb he "damned himself, and all his line," bringing original sin on humankind.
Roman goddess of love and the planet of the third sphere of Heaven, home of souls who loved ardently. The ancients wrongly worshipped Venus as the source of mad love.
In the old astronomy, a small circle on which Venus was thought to ride within its sphere. The ancients believed Venus, "wheeling in the third epicycle," rayed love down on men.
In myth, the mother of Venus. The ancient peoples worshipped her along with Venus as part of their error.
The boy-god of love, son of Venus, who in legend sat in Dido's lap to inflame her love for Aeneas. He was worshipped by the ancients as Venus's son.
The order of angels (Principalities, in Dante's scheme the Thrones) who move the sphere of Venus. The souls there wheel "in one ring" with them.

Charles Martel of Anjou, heir to Naples, Hungary, and Provence, who died young. In the sphere of Venus he greets Dante warmly, laments the misrule of his family, and explains how good fathers can have bad sons.
A river that joins the Rhone in Provence. Charles Martel names the Provencal land that awaited his rule.
An ancient name for Sicily, "dark with smoke" from the volcano Etna. Charles laments that misrule lost his line its rightful kingship there.
A monstrous giant whom myth buried under Sicily, traditionally blamed for Etna's smoke. Dante corrects this: the smoke comes "not from Typhoeus, but from rising sulphur."
The chief city of Sicily, which rose in revolt (the Sicilian Vespers) crying "Death! Death!" against the hated French (Angevin) misrule.
Rudolph I of Habsburg, Holy Roman Emperor and grandfather, through marriage, of Charles Martel's heirs. Charles names him with himself as ancestor of Sicily's rightful kings.
The Spanish region whose grasping followers, Charles warns, burdened his brother Robert's grasping rule of Naples.
The ancient Athenian lawgiver, cited by Charles as an example of a man born to legislate — proof that human gifts are diverse by divine design.
The Persian king famed for his great army, named by Charles as a born warrior — another example of diverse natures.
The biblical priest-king of Salem, cited by Charles as one born to the priesthood, illustrating that people are fitted to different callings.

glossary.term: the man who flew through the air and lost his son in falling
glossary.gloss: Daedalus, the legendary inventor who built wings and flew, while his son Icarus fell to his death. Charles names him as a born craftsman among diverse human types.
The biblical son of Isaac, twin of Jacob, who "differs in the seed" from his brother. Charles cites the twins to show heaven shapes characters differently even from one cradle.
The biblical patriarch, twin brother of Esau, used by Charles to illustrate how differently the heavens shape two children of the same parents.
Romulus, founder of Rome, said to spring "from a father so base he is given to Mars" — i.e. his lowly origin was dignified by calling Mars his father. An example of nature differing from parentage.
God, the supreme intelligence whose providence orders the heavens and the natures they shape. Charles argues this Mind cannot be flawed, so the heavens' effects are not in vain.
Clemence, kinswoman (wife or daughter) of Charles Martel, whom Dante addresses at the opening of Canto IX as he reports the wrongs Charles foretold for his line.
The fourth sphere of Heaven, home of the wise — theologians, doctors, and philosophers, who appear as circling rings of brilliant lights. Dante enters it in Canto X.
Cunizza da Romano, a noblewoman known for her many loves, here shining in the sphere of Venus. She forgives herself her amorous past and prophesies disasters for the Italian March.
The heart of Venice, named to mark the bounds of the corrupt Italian region (the March of Treviso) that Cunizza describes.
Two rivers of northeastern Italy that, with Rialto, bound the corrupt region Cunizza comes from and condemns.
Ezzelino da Romano, Cunizza's brutal brother, born on a hill near Romano, whose tyranny "fell on that whole region like a war." A dream foretold his birth as a firebrand.
An order of angels, the "mirrors" through which God's judgment shines down on the blessed of Venus. Cunizza says they let her speak her prophecies with assurance.
Folco of Marseilles, a famed troubadour-poet of passionate love who later became a bishop. In the sphere of Venus he speaks of repented passion turned to joy in God, and denounces Church corruption.
Two rivers, in Spain and Italy, marking the bounds of the Mediterranean valley where Folco lived. The Magra parts Tuscany from Genoa.
A North African coastal town (modern Béjaïa, Algeria) that shares nearly the same sunrise and sunset as Marseilles, the town Folco came from.
Dido, queen of Carthage, who burned with love for Aeneas, betraying the memory of her dead husband Sychaeus and Aeneas's wife Creusa. Folco compares his own youthful ardor to hers.
The first wife of Aeneas, lost in the fall of Troy. Dido's love for Aeneas wronged Creusa as well as Sychaeus.
Phyllis, a Thracian princess (of Mount Rhodope) who killed herself when deceived by her lover Demophoon. Folco names her among famous burning loves.
The son of Theseus who deceived and abandoned the Thracian princess Phyllis, driving her to suicide.
The captive princess Hercules loved, whose memory the jealousy over her brought about the hero's death.
The harlot of Jericho who hid Joshua's spies and so aided Israel's conquest. She shines in the sphere of Venus as the first soul carried to Heaven by Christ's triumph over Hell.
The Old Testament leader who, after Moses, conquered the Holy Land. Rahab aided his "first proud deed" at Jericho and so won her place in Heaven.
The conical shadow the earth casts into space, whose point was thought to reach as far as the sphere of Venus. Rahab was raised "into this heaven, where the cone of shadow comes to its point."
The florin, the gold coin of Florence stamped with a lily, blamed for corrupting the Church and clergy with greed. Folco says Florence "mints and scatters" it.
The books of Church law, studied (for the profit they brought) at the expense of the Gospel and the Doctors of the Church. Folco condemns clergy who pore over them while the Scriptures rot.
Diana, goddess of the moon. Dante compares the ring of dancing souls in the Sun to the halo ("belt") sometimes seen around the moon in misty air.
Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominican Order (the "holy flock"). Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican, calls himself one of Dominic's lambs; Dominic is praised at length as the second "prince" of the Church.
Albertus Magnus, the great German scholar and teacher (and a saint), Thomas Aquinas's master. He stands at Thomas's right hand in the sphere of the Sun.
Saint Thomas Aquinas, the towering medieval theologian, who names and introduces the other wise souls in the ring around Dante in the sphere of the Sun.
The 12th-century monk who systematized canon law, harmonizing the courts of civil and Church law. He shines among the wise in the sphere of the Sun.
Peter Lombard, author of the Sentences, the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages, who like the poor widow gave his whole treasure to the Church. One of the lights in the Sun.
King Solomon, "the most beautiful among us," set in the ring of the wise for his unequalled God-given wisdom — "if the truth be true, no second ever rose to see so far."
Dionysius the Areopagite, the supposed author who, "in the flesh below, looked deepest into the nature of the angels," mapping the angelic orders. One of the wise in the Sun.

glossary.term: the advocate of the Christian centuries
glossary.gloss: Paulus Orosius (or, by some readings, an early Christian defender) whose history defended the faith and "supplied even Augustine." One of the lights in the Sun.
Saint Augustine of Hippo, the great Church Father, whose work was aided by the Christian apologist named here among the wise.
Boethius, author of The Consolation of Philosophy, "who shows the lying world for what it is." His body lies in Cieldauro in Pavia; he came home to Heaven from martyrdom and exile.
The church of San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro in Pavia, where the body of Boethius lies buried. Dante names it to identify the eighth light in the Sun.
Saint Isidore of Seville, the encyclopedic scholar, named among the burning lights of wisdom in the sphere of the Sun.
The Venerable Bede, the English monk and historian-scholar, listed among the wise souls in the Sun.
Richard of Saint Victor, the medieval mystic who "in his contemplation rose to more than human." One of the lights in the sphere of the Sun.
Siger of Brabant, a philosopher who "lectured in the Street of Straw" (the university quarter of Paris) and reasoned out unpopular truths. His light closes the first ring of the wise.
The Rue du Fouarre in Paris, the street of the university lecture halls where Siger of Brabant taught philosophy.
The Church (and, by extension, the soul) wedded to Christ. Dante compares the dancing wheel of souls to a clock that wakes the Bride to sing her morning praise to her Spouse.
Poverty personified as the bride whom Saint Francis married. "Widowed" since Christ, scorned by all for eleven hundred years, she found in Francis her devoted lover. Central to Canto XI.

Saint Francis of Assisi, founder of the Franciscan Order, whose life is told in Canto XI as a love story: he wedded Lady Poverty, defied his father, won papal approval, and received the stigmata. The "seraphic" prince of the Church.
Saint Ubaldo of Gubbio, the holy bishop whose chosen hilltop helps Dante locate Assisi, the fertile slope where Francis ("a sun") rose upon the world.
A central Italian city near Assisi, named (with its Porta Sole gate) to fix the geography of Francis's birthplace.
Two towns near Assisi, said to grieve "under their heavy yoke," used to locate the slope where Saint Francis was born.
The hometown of Saint Francis. Dante says calling the place "Assisi" says too little — it should be called "Orient," the East, since a sun (Francis) rose there.
The great river of India, in the far East where the sun rises. Dante says Francis rose on the world "the way our sun climbs sometimes from the Ganges."
A poor fisherman who, owning nothing, was unafraid when Julius Caesar ("who once struck terror into all the world") came to his hut. Dante cites him as Poverty found fearless even before Caesar.
Bernard of Quintavalle, the first follower of Saint Francis, who "kicked his shoes off and ran" to join the life of poverty.
Brother Giles, an early companion of Saint Francis who went barefoot after "the bridegroom" (Francis), drawn by love of Lady Poverty.
The wealthy cloth-merchant father of Saint Francis, against whose wishes Francis embraced poverty. Francis felt no shame at being his son.
Pope Innocent III, from whose hands Saint Francis received the first official approval ("the first seal") of his Order.
Pope Honorius III, through whom "the Eternal Spirit crowned a second time" the will of Francis, giving his Order its second, fuller confirmation.
The stigmata — the wounds of Christ's crucifixion miraculously imprinted on Francis on the rock of La Verna, between the Tiber and the Arno, which his body bore for two years.
Two central Italian rivers framing Mount La Verna, the "bare rock" where Saint Francis received the stigmata from Christ.
The Church, figured as the ship of Saint Peter. Dante says Saint Dominic was the fit partner who, like Francis, helped keep "Peter's boat steady on its course."
Saint Francis, called "our Patriarch" by Thomas — the founding father whose followers, if faithful, are "loaded with good cargo," though his flock has grown greedy and strayed.
God, the unchanging divine radiance into which the blessed gaze and in which they read all truth. Thomas says he reads Dante's thoughts by gazing into it.
Saints Francis and Dominic, the two leaders God appointed to guide the Church — one "all seraphic in his ardor" (Francis), the other "a splendor of cherubic light" for his wisdom (Dominic).
The horn-shaped tip of the Little Dipper (Ursa Minor), ending near the pole star around which the heavens seem to turn.
Ariadne, daughter of King Minos of Crete. The crown she wore was set in the sky as the constellation Corona Borealis, which Dante uses as an image for the ring of lights.
A sluggish, slow-moving river in Tuscany. Dante contrasts its crawling current with the swiftest sphere of heaven to stress how far the souls' dance outpaces anything earthly.

glossary.term: Three Persons in the divine nature
glossary.gloss: The Christian Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as one God. The souls sing this instead of pagan praise.
Saint Thomas Aquinas, the speaking light, who has just praised Saint Francis (the 'beggar' of God). Here he turns to clear up a second doubt, about Solomon.
A reference to Adam, from whose rib Eve was made in Genesis. Adam, created directly by God, had perfect human nature.
Christ, whose side was pierced by a soldier's lance at the crucifixion. His perfect human nature, like Adam's, came straight from God.
The nine orders of angels (or the nine heavenly spheres) through which God's creating light passes, like rays caught in a mirror, before reaching the lower, perishable world.
The biblical king of Israel famed for his God-given wisdom. He is the bright fifth light here; Aquinas explains that his unequalled wisdom was kingly practical wisdom, not abstract knowledge.
An ancient Greek philosopher. Dante lists him among thinkers who 'set out and knew not where' as a warning against hasty, overconfident reasoning.
An ancient Greek philosopher, named alongside Parmenides as an example of flawed reasoning to be wary of.
An ancient Greek thinker who tried to square the circle by faulty method. Listed as a caution against careless reasoning.
An early Christian heretic who denied the distinct Persons of the Trinity. Dante calls such heretics swords that twisted Scripture's true face.
An early Christian heretic who denied that Christ was fully God. Named with Sabellius as one who distorted Scripture.
Stand-in names for ordinary people (like 'John Doe and Jane Doe'). Dante warns them not to presume they can read God's hidden judgment of who is saved or damned.
The Trinity again: one God in three Persons, praised by the souls in a hymn. The numbers play on unity and threeness.
The angel Gabriel's gentle greeting to the Virgin Mary at the Annunciation. Dante likens the modest voice of the speaking soul to that hushed, reverent tone.
The eternal joy and celebration of the blessed in Paradise. As long as it lasts, the souls' radiant light will keep shining around them.
The Christian belief that at the end of time the blessed will get their bodies back, glorified, making their joy more complete. The souls long for this reunion.
The planet Mars, the fifth heaven, into which Dante is now lifted. It glows redder than usual to mark his ascent.
An ancient name for the sun (the sun god). Dante cries it out as a figure for God, who adorns the souls with such red splendor.
The Milky Way, the band of countless faint and bright stars across the night sky. Dante compares it to the cross of lights blazing in Mars.
The shape of the Cross, traced out by the gathered souls within the planet Mars; on it Christ flashes like lightning.
In the heaven of Mars, the warrior-souls of the faith arrange themselves into a great glowing cross, on which the figure of Christ blazes. This is the sphere of those who fought for God.
Virgil, the Roman poet of the Aeneid, whom Dante reveres as his chief poetic master. 'If we can trust him' nods to his account of Anchises greeting Aeneas.
In classical myth, the blessed region of the afterlife where good souls dwell. There Anchises met his son Aeneas.
Dante's great-great-grandfather, a Florentine knight who died on Crusade. He is the radiant ancestor who speaks to Dante across these cantos, praises old Florence, and later foretells Dante's exile.
A legendary Assyrian king famous for soft, decadent luxury. His name stands for the indulgence and excess that, Cacciaguida says, old Florence had not yet known.
A hill overlooking Florence. Cacciaguida says Florence's rising extravagance ('Uccellatoio') had not yet outdone Rome's ('Montemalo')—and what overshoots in its rise will fall the harder.
Monte Mario, a hill near Rome. Used as the measure of Roman grandeur that Florentine excess was beginning to surpass.
A respected old Florentine citizen, remembered for plain, unpretentious dress (a simple leather belt). A symbol of the city's lost modesty.
Two old Florentine families cited as examples of the city's former simple, hardworking virtue.
Mentioned as the place Florentine husbands now go off to for trade, leaving their wives behind—a sign of changed, unsettled times.
A notoriously immoral Florentine woman of Dante's day. Her name stands for the moral decline of the present, contrasted with old Roman virtue.
A corrupt Florentine lawyer and politician of Dante's time, named beside Cianghella as a sign of how far the city had fallen.
A Roman statesman famous for civic virtue and humility, who returned to his farm after holding power. A model of integrity, set against Florence's corrupt figures.
The Baptistery of San Giovanni (Saint John) in Florence, where Cacciaguida (and later Dante) was baptized. 'The sheepfold of Saint John' is the city under its patron.
One of Cacciaguida's brothers, named as he recounts his family.
Another of Cacciaguida's brothers, named in his account of his kin.
The river-valley region of northern Italy from which Cacciaguida's wife came; the family surname (Alighieri) was drawn from her family's place.
Conrad III, the Holy Roman Emperor whom Cacciaguida followed on Crusade and who knighted him. Cacciaguida died fighting the infidels in his service.
Queen of King Arthur's court in romance. Dante recalls the moment a lady-in-waiting coughed at Guinevere's first flirtation with Lancelot; Beatrice's smile is compared to that knowing reaction.
Small towns in the Florentine countryside. Cacciaguida complains that newcomers from such places have diluted the city's once-pure citizenry.
Two villages near Florence. Cacciaguida wishes the city had kept its boundaries modest out here rather than absorbing corrupt newcomers.
A town whose 'boor' (Baldo d'Aguglione, a grasping Florentine politician) Cacciaguida names with contempt as one of the corrupting newcomers.
A town near Florence; 'that man from Signa' (Fazio dei Morubaldini) is named as a sharp-eyed fraud among the city's bad new citizens.
A castle town whose people moved to Florence to trade and lend at interest. Cacciaguida says, but for the Church's meddling, such families would still be back home.
The Counts Guidi, a powerful feudal family. Cacciaguida notes that places like Montemurlo would still be theirs in a less disrupted order.
A Florentine family of newcomers turned powerful, leaders of the White faction. Cacciaguida says they belonged out in Acone's parish, not inside the walls.
A Florentine noble family. Buondelmonte de' Buondelmonti's broken marriage promise sparked the deadly Guelph–Ghibelline feud; Cacciaguida laments the bloodshed it began.
Once-thriving Italian cities now fallen to ruin. Cacciaguida cites them to show that even great cities and bloodlines die.
Two declining Italian towns, named with Luni and Urbisaglia as proof that nothing earthly lasts forever.
One of the great old Florentine families now faded, recited in Cacciaguida's roll call of the city's vanished nobility.
An eminent old Florentine family, ancestors of Count Guido and the famous Bellincione. Part of Cacciaguida's catalogue of the great houses of early Florence.
The golden balls on the coat of arms of the Lamberti (or, by tradition, an old Florentine house), here a symbol of the noble families who made Florence great.
The fleur-de-lis emblem on Florence's banner. Cacciaguida recalls a time when it was never reversed in defeat nor stained red by civil bloodshed.
Hugh of Brandenburg (the 'great baron'), the marquis whose feast on Saint Thomas's day Florence still keeps; he had knighted several old families.

Mother of Phaethon. He went to her to confirm the taunt that he was not really the Sun-god's son; the story 'still makes fathers wary of their sons.' Dante likens his own anxious request to Phaethon's.
Christ, who 'takes away the sins of the world.' Cacciaguida speaks plainly, not in the riddling oracles common before Christ's coming.
In Greek myth, the innocent son driven out of Athens by the lies of his stepmother Phaedra. Cacciaguida compares Dante's coming unjust exile from Florence to this.

glossary.term: where Christ is bought and sold
glossary.gloss: Rome, the seat of a corrupt papacy. Cacciaguida foretells that Dante's exile is being plotted there, where holy offices are trafficked for money.
Dante's banishment from Florence, foretold here by Cacciaguida: he will lose all he loves, taste 'how salt is another man's bread,' and learn the hardship of dependence.
Bartolommeo della Scala of Verona, Dante's first generous host in exile, whose family bore an eagle ('the holy bird') over a ladder on its arms.

glossary.term: the holy bird on the ladder
glossary.gloss: The coat of arms of the della Scala family of Verona: the imperial eagle above a ladder (scala). It identifies Dante's Lombard host.
Mars, the planet of this heaven, said to have stamped a future patron of Dante (Can Grande della Scala) with the temperament for great deeds.
Pope Clement V, a Frenchman from Gascony, who would betray the emperor Henry VII ('the noble Henry'). The prophecy dates the young patron's first sparks of greatness.
Henry VII, the Holy Roman Emperor on whom Dante pinned his hopes; the Gascon pope Clement V would cheat and undermine him.
The fifth heaven, the sphere of Mars, where warrior-souls of the faith are gathered on the great glowing Cross.
Judas Maccabeus, the Jewish hero who fought to free his people and rededicate the Temple. His light spins like a joyful top on the Cross.
William of Orange and Renouard (Rainouart), heroes of medieval French epic who fought the infidels. Two more lights on the Cross of Mars.
Godfrey of Bouillon, leader of the First Crusade who captured Jerusalem. Counted among the warriors for the faith.
Jupiter, the sixth heaven, into which Dante now rises. It is the sphere of just rulers; its white light marks moderation and justice.
Latin for 'Love justice'—the opening words spelled out by the souls of Jupiter, the heaven of just rulers. The full motto is 'Love justice, you who judge the earth.'
The grand figure formed by the just-ruler souls in the sixth heaven; symbol of imperial Rome and of God's justice, it speaks to Dante about salvation and earthly kings.
The two great apostles martyred at Rome ('this vineyard'). Dante reproaches corrupt popes who undo the Church those saints died to build.

glossary.term: the one who chose to live alone
glossary.gloss: John the Baptist, who lived in the desert and was beheaded for a girl's (Salome's) dance. Dante mocks a greedy pope who cares only for the saint stamped on the gold florin, not for Peter or Paul.
The river marking the far edge of the known world (India). The eagle imagines a virtuous man born there who never heard of Christ, to raise the puzzle of divine justice.
Lucifer, the highest of created angels, who fell through pride for not waiting for God's light. The eagle cites him to show no creature can grasp all of God.
God's perfect judgment, which human sight can no more fathom than the eye can see the bottom of the open sea. A central theme of the eagle's speech.
A figure for the virtuous non-Christian who, at the Last Judgment, will condemn false Christians who cried 'Christ!' but did not live by him.
Another non-Christian people who, the eagle says, will shame Christian kings by pointing to the record of their disgraceful deeds.
Albert of Austria, Holy Roman Emperor, whose misdeed (laying waste the realm of Prague/Bohemia) will be written in the book of kings' shame.
Charles II of Anjou (King of Naples and titular King of Jerusalem), lame and morally worse. His one virtue will be marked 'I' (one), his vices 'M' (a thousand).
Sicily, with its volcano Etna, where Anchises died. Its ruler (Frederick of Aragon) is condemned for greed and cowardice.
Anchises, Aeneas's father, died in Sicily ('the Island of Fire') during their voyage—a learned reference fixing the place.
A kingdom the eagle calls 'happy' if only it stops letting itself be wronged by bad rule.
Two cities of Cyprus that 'wail and rage' under their brutish French ruler (of the house of Lusignan). Closing examples of misgoverned realms.

glossary.term: the singer of the Holy Spirit
glossary.gloss: King David, who composed the Psalms and danced before the Ark of the Covenant as it was carried from city to city. He forms the eye of the eagle.

glossary.term: the one who comforted the widow
glossary.gloss: The Emperor Trajan, in legend, who stopped to do justice for a poor widow whose son was killed. He is one of the five lights in the eagle's eyebrow.

glossary.term: put death off by true repentance
glossary.gloss: King Hezekiah of the Bible, whose sincere prayer won him fifteen more years of life. One of the just souls in the eagle's brow.

glossary.term: turned Greek by yielding to the shepherd
glossary.gloss: The Emperor Constantine, who (in medieval belief) moved the empire's capital east to Constantinople, 'turning Greek,' out of deference to the pope. A well-meant act with bad results.
William II 'the Good' of Sicily, a just king mourned by his land. One of the souls in the eagle's eye.
A minor figure from Virgil's Aeneid, called the most just of the Trojans. Dante astonishingly places this pagan among the saved, by a secret grace, as one of the eagle's eye-lights.
God's eternal choosing of who is saved—its 'root' lies hidden even from the blessed. The eagle warns mortals not to presume to judge it.
The three theological virtues—Faith, Hope, and Charity—seen at the right wheel of the chariot in an earlier vision; they served as Ripheus's baptism a thousand years before Christian baptism existed.
Saturn, the seventh heaven, into which Dante now rises—the sphere of contemplative souls. Here, for the first time, Beatrice does not smile and no music sounds, because Dante could not bear them.
The constellation Leo, under which Saturn is currently positioned. Its 'force' mingles with Saturn's downward rays.
Saturn, the planet, named for the god-king of the mythical Golden Age, when (the poets said) the world was innocent and 'no wickedness was left alive.'
The golden ladder (Jacob's Ladder) rising through the heaven of Saturn, up which the contemplative souls climb toward God. Dante cannot see its top.
God's governing care over all things. The contemplative souls' free love is enough to follow it exactly, descending the ladder to greet Dante.
A high mountain ridge in the Italian Apennines, near Dante's homeland. On its slope stood the hermitage where Peter Damian served God in solitude.
An 11th-century hermit, monk, and reforming cardinal, here a contemplative soul in the heaven of Saturn. He recalls his austere hermit life and bitterly attacks the worldliness of the clergy.

glossary.term: the house of Our Lady on the Adriatic
glossary.gloss: The monastery of Santa Maria (Pomposa or Fonte Avellana) by the Adriatic Sea, where Peter Damian lived as 'Peter the Sinner.'
The cardinal's red hat. Peter Damian was reluctantly dragged into that office, which he says 'only ever passes from bad to worse.'
Saint Peter the apostle (Cephas is his name in Aramaic). Peter Damian recalls how Peter walked lean and barefoot—unlike the bloated, pampered prelates of the present.

glossary.term: the great Vessel of the Holy Spirit
glossary.gloss: Saint Paul, called a 'chosen vessel' of the Spirit. Like Peter, he lived in poverty—a rebuke to the luxury of modern shepherds.
aliases: the Vessel of the Holy Spirit

glossary.gloss: The mountain of Monte Cassino in Italy, where Saint Benedict founded his great monastery, converting the pagan locals. He speaks here as a contemplative soul.
The 6th-century father of Western monasticism, who founded Monte Cassino and wrote the monastic Rule. The brightest pearl of the contemplatives, he laments how monks have abandoned his Rule.
An early Christian desert hermit, a model of the contemplative life. Saint Benedict names him among the souls of contemplation here.
Saint Romuald, founder of the Camaldolese order of hermit-monks. Named beside Macarius among the contemplative souls.

The Empyrean, the highest heaven beyond space and motion, where God and all the blessed dwell and where every longing is fulfilled. Benedict says Dante's wish to see his face unveiled waits for there.
The biblical patriarch who dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven thronged with angels. Benedict says the contemplatives' stairway is that very ladder, now empty of climbers.
The Rule of Saint Benedict, the guide for monastic life. Benedict laments it is now 'a dead letter, a waste of paper,' ignored by corrupt monks.
The biblical miracle of the river Jordan turning back its flow (and the Red Sea parting). Benedict says these were lesser marvels than the rescue God could yet work for the corrupt Church.
The zodiac sign Gemini (the Twins), which Dante now enters in the eighth heaven of the fixed stars. He was born under Gemini and credits it for his genius.
The Moon (the goddess Diana, daughter of Latona). Looking down from the heaven of fixed stars, Dante sees the Moon clear of the dark patches that once puzzled him.
A Titan, father of the Sun in myth. 'The face of your son, Hyperion' means the Sun, which Dante can now look at bearably from this height.
Mothers of Mercury and Venus in myth; here their names stand for the planets Mercury and Venus, seen circling near the Sun.
The planet Jupiter, moderate and temperate, seen moving between his 'father' Saturn and his 'son' Mars in Dante's downward survey of the spheres.
The earth, seen tiny and pitiful from on high. Dante calls it the small patch of ground 'that makes us so fierce,' and smiles at how mean it looks.
The triumphant host of the blessed—the saints gathered in Christ's victory—revealed to Dante in the heaven of the fixed stars.
aliases: the armies of Christ in His triumph

glossary.gloss: A name for the Moon-goddess Diana. Dante pictures her smiling among the stars ('the eternal nymphs') on a clear full-moon night—an image for the one Sun (Christ) outshining all.
Christ, who blazes above thousands of lamps (the blessed) and lights them all, as the earthly sun lights the stars. Dante cannot bear the direct sight of him.
Titles of Christ. Beatrice says it is the very Wisdom and Power of God that opened the road between heaven and earth—what now overwhelms Dante's sight.
One of the nine Muses, patron of sacred song. Dante says even all the Muses' sweetest powers could not capture a thousandth of Beatrice's holy smile.
The Virgin Mary, in whom the Word of God became flesh. In the garden of the blessed she is the supreme flower; the apostles are the lilies.
The apostles, whose example ('scent') pointed the way to the good road. Set beside Mary, 'the Rose,' in the flowering garden of the saints.
The Virgin Mary, the name Dante invokes morning and evening. Her glory, 'the greatest fire' among the blessed, draws his whole soul.
The archangel Gabriel, who descends as a crowning flame of fire and song, circling Mary and declaring himself the angelic love that surrounds the joy born of her womb.
Latin for 'Queen of Heaven'—a hymn to the Virgin Mary that the blessed sing with overwhelming sweetness as they reach toward her ascending light.
An image of earthly life as exile, far from the heavenly homeland. The blessed won their treasure 'while weeping in the exile of Babylon,' leaving worldly gold behind.
Saint Peter, given the keys of heaven by Christ. He triumphs among the blessed beneath Christ and Mary, with the saints of the Old and New Testaments.

glossary.term: the ancient council and the new
glossary.gloss: The saints of the Old Testament ('ancient') and of the New ('new')—the whole company of the redeemed gathered in Christ's triumph.
Dante's name for Beatrice, his heavenly guide. He uses it throughout these cantos as a term of reverence and love.
The great vision opening Canto XXIII in which Christ appears in radiant glory above the redeemed, like a victorious general leading his triumphant army.
A poetic name for the stars, pictured as nymphs attending the moon-goddess Trivia and painting the night sky.
The Virgin Mary, called a star that conquers in heaven as she did on earth.
The Virgin Mary, likened to the sapphire (the bluest, most precious gem) that adorns the highest heaven.
A title for the Virgin Mary, addressed by the angel Gabriel as she rises to follow her Son into the Empyrean.
Christ, pictured as the Lamb of God whose 'great supper' (the heavenly banquet) feeds and forever satisfies the blessed.
The chief apostle, keeper of the keys of heaven, who in Canto XXIV examines Dante on the virtue of Faith. He is the rock on whom the Church is built and the first of Christ's vicars.
aliases: the first soul that the first Power ever made

glossary.gloss: The first of the three theological virtues, on which Peter examines Dante. Dante defines it (after Saint Paul) as the substance of things hoped for and the evidence of things not seen.
A graduate student in the medieval university who arms himself with arguments while waiting for the master to pose the question; Dante's image for himself awaiting Peter's examination.
Saint Paul, whose Letter to the Hebrews supplies the definition of faith Dante recites to Peter; Paul, with Peter, set Rome on the road of the Faith.
aliases: he who with you set Rome on the good road

glossary.term: the old parchments and the new
glossary.gloss: The Old and New Testaments of the Bible, poured out by the Holy Spirit, which Dante calls the proof of his faith.
A formal logical argument in which a conclusion follows from premises; Dante calls Scripture itself the syllogism that proved his faith to him.
Peter's metaphor for faith, tested like a coin for its alloy and weight; Dante answers that he carries it bright and round in his purse, sure of its minting.
The third Person of the Trinity, whose grace pours over Scripture; in Canto XXIV its rain is what convinced Dante of the truth of the Bible.
The Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one in essence yet three, which Dante professes in his confession of faith to Peter.
aliases: three colors and of one dimension

glossary.gloss: The apostle Saint James, called the great lord of Galicia (his shrine at Santiago de Compostela), who in Canto XXV examines Dante on the virtue of Hope.
The region of northwest Spain where pilgrims crowd to the shrine of Saint James at Santiago de Compostela.
The second theological virtue, on which James examines Dante. Dante defines it as the sure expectation of glory to come, the work of grace and prior merit.
The Church still struggling on earth (as opposed to the Church Triumphant in heaven). Beatrice says it has no child of greater hope than Dante.

glossary.term: out of Egypt to see Jerusalem
glossary.gloss: An image for the soul's journey from the bondage of earthly life (Egypt) to the peace of heaven (Jerusalem), granted to Dante before his death.

glossary.term: chief singer to the highest captain
glossary.gloss: King David, author of the Psalms, the first to instill hope in Dante's heart; the 'highest captain' is God.
The Old Testament prophet, cited by Dante on hope: that each blessed soul, clothed in its own land, shall wear a double garment (body and soul reunited).
Saint John the Evangelist, James's fellow apostle, who in his Revelation speaks of the robes of white worn by the blessed; cited by Dante on hope.

The apostle and evangelist Saint John, who lay on Christ's breast at the Last Supper and was chosen from the cross to care for Mary. In Canto XXV he is the third examining light; Dante is dazzled trying to see whether John's body was taken up to heaven.
aliases: the one who lay on the breast

glossary.gloss: Christ, pictured as the pelican believed to feed its young with its own blood, a symbol of Christ's sacrifice; John 'lay on the breast' of this Pelican.
Body and soul; only Christ and Mary, Dante is told, have risen to heaven already with both, so John's body still lies on earth.
The zodiac constellation Cancer, opposite Capricorn; Dante uses it to measure brightness and season in his astronomical similes.
The disciple who, in the Book of Acts, laid hands on the blinded Saul (Paul) and restored his sight; Beatrice's gaze is said to have the same healing power for Dante's dazzled eyes.
The third theological virtue (charity), on which John examines Dante in Canto XXVI. Dante answers that all things, philosophy and Scripture alike, draw his highest love to God.
The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, a title for God as the beginning and end of all things; Dante names God so when professing his love.
God, pictured as the gardener of creation; Dante loves all created things (the leaves of the garden) in measure of the good God gave them.
The Garden of Eden, the earthly paradise from which Adam fell and where Beatrice's Lady prepared Dante's long ascent.
aliases: the high garden where this Lady

glossary.gloss: A Hebrew name for God; Adam tells Dante that the name of the Highest Good was first 'I' (or Ya) and later 'El,' since human language is always changing.

glossary.term: the mountain that rises highest from the sea
glossary.gloss: The Mount of Purgatory, on whose summit lies Eden, where Adam lived briefly in innocence and then in sin.
In Canto XXVII all Paradise sings 'Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,' the doxology praising the Trinity.
Peter's denunciation of Pope Boniface VIII, whom he condemns for corrupting the papacy and leaving Peter's seat empty in the sight of God.
aliases: my place, my place, my place

glossary.gloss: Satan (Lucifer), who fell from heaven and now takes comfort in the corruption of the Church on earth.
Early popes and martyrs (successors of Peter) who shed their blood for the Church, named by Peter as models against the corrupt papacy of his day.

glossary.term: Sixtus and Pius, Urban and Calixtus
glossary.gloss: Early popes and martyrs who poured out their blood for the faith, contrasted by Peter with greedy later pontiffs.
The Church, pictured as Christ's bride, founded not to be sold for gold but built on the blood of the martyrs.
aliases: the bride Christ made his own

glossary.gloss: The corrupt popes John XXII (from Cahors) and Clement V (from Gascony), accused of being ready to drink the Church's blood for greed.
The zodiac constellation Capricorn (the Goat), used in a seasonal simile for the time when snow falls.
The city at the far western edge of the known world (the Strait of Gibraltar); Dante looks down past it to the wild track of Ulysses' final voyage.
The princess of myth whom Zeus, disguised as a bull, carried off across the sea; her shore (Phoenicia/the eastern Mediterranean) marks the eastern limit of Dante's downward view.
aliases: where Europa made herself sweet cargo

glossary.gloss: The earth, seen from the heights of heaven as small and humble as a farmyard threshing-floor.
The constellation Gemini (the twins Castor and Pollux, sons of Leda), the sign under which Dante was born; Beatrice's gaze drives him up from it into the highest moving heaven.
The Primum Mobile (First Moving Sphere), the ninth and swiftest heaven, whose only 'where' is the Mind of God and which sets time and motion for all the rest.

glossary.term: the fair daughter of him who brings the morning
glossary.gloss: Humankind, the offspring of the sun (a poetic figure for human nature), whose innocence darkens as it grows from childhood into sin.
The infinitely bright, dimensionless point of light that Dante sees as the image of God in Canto XXVIII; all the heavens and nature depend on it, and the nine angelic orders wheel around it.
The nine ranks of angels Dante sees as rings of fire whirling round the divine Point: Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones; Dominions, Virtues, Powers; Principalities, Archangels, Angels.
The highest order of angels, the ring closest to God, burning with the most love; first of the nine choirs.
The second order of angels, paired with the Seraphim in the first triad, distinguished by the depth of their knowledge of God.
The first order of the second triad of angels.
The second order of the second triad of angels (distinct from the moral virtues).
The third order of the second triad of angels.
An order of the third and lowest triad of angels.
An order of the third and lowest triad of angels, ranked just above the plain Angels.
The ninth and lowest order of the angelic hierarchy, whose dance closes the rings around the divine Point.
In medieval cosmology, the angelic mind assigned to move and govern each heavenly sphere; Beatrice matches each order's power to the sphere it turns.
Iris, the rainbow, messenger of the goddess Juno; even the whole rainbow would be too narrow to ring the wide seventh angelic circle.
Pope Gregory the Great, who ordered the angelic ranks differently from Dionysius and (Dante imagines) smiled at his own error on reaching heaven.
The sun and the moon (Apollo and Diana, children of the goddess Latona), pictured balanced on opposite horizons in Canto XXIX's opening simile.
The zodiac constellation Aries; used in Dante's astronomical similes to mark the position of the sun.
The zodiac constellation Libra; used with Aries to picture sun and moon balanced on the horizon.
God, whose love overflowed in the act of creation, opening 'into new loves' (the angels) outside of time. A name for the creative God of Canto XXIX.
The two basic principles of created being in medieval philosophy; Dante says God made pure form (the angels), pure matter, and the two joined, all at once like three arrows from one bow.
aliases: Form and matter, both apart and joined

glossary.gloss: In Aristotelian-medieval terms, being fully realized with no unfulfilled potential; the angels, at the summit of creation, are of pure act. Pure potential holds the lowest place.
Saint Jerome, the Bible translator, who held that the angels were created long before the rest of the world; Beatrice corrects him in Canto XXIX.
The rebellion of Lucifer and his angels, which (Beatrice says) happened almost instantly after creation; the faithful angels who stayed humble keep wheeling for love.
God, whose single light pours into the angels and is received by each in its own degree, splintering into countless reflections.
A figure for greedy, fraud-living friars who fatten themselves on the credulity of the people, named after the pig that was the emblem of the Antonine order.
Common Florentine names (like 'Tom or Dick'), used by Beatrice to say Florence has even more foolish preachers' fables than it has men with these names.
Noon; Dante opens Canto XXX with an astronomical figure marking the hour as the Triumph of saints fades from his sight.

glossary.term: the heaven that is pure light
glossary.gloss: The Empyrean, the highest heaven beyond the physical spheres: pure intellectual light, full of love and joy, the true dwelling of God, the angels, and all the blessed.

The amber-gold river of living light, flowing between flowering banks, that Dante first sees in the Empyrean; living sparks leap from it onto the flowers. When he drinks of it, the river reveals itself as the round Celestial Rose.
The glittering sparks (souls or angels) that leap in and out of the River of Light like living jewels; later understood as the blessed and the angels themselves.

The vast white Rose of Paradise: rank on rank of the blessed seated in petals rising in tiers around God, breathing praise up to him like a flower to the sun. The supreme image of the communion of saints.
aliases: the Rose where its outermost petals spread

glossary.gloss: The blessed souls of the Celestial Rose, clothed in shining white; their gathering is nearly complete, with few seats left to fill.
The Holy Roman Emperor Henry VII, whom Dante hoped would set Italy right; a throne in the Rose already awaits him, though he will come before Italy is ready and die without succeeding.
Pope Boniface VIII (born at Anagni) or Clement V; Beatrice foretells that the false pope opposing Henry will be thrust down even below the simonist Boniface.
The constellation of the Great Bear (Ursa Major), into which the nymph Callisto was transformed; her 'son' is the nearby Little Bear. A figure for the far northern lands of the barbarians.
The great basilica and palace in Rome, here standing for the height of Rome's earthly glory, which amazed visiting barbarians.
The cloth believed to bear the imprint of Christ's face, a famous Roman relic; pilgrims came from far to gaze on it, an image Dante uses for his own wonder at Bernard.

Bernard of Clairvaux, the great contemplative and devotee of the Virgin Mary, who replaces Beatrice as Dante's final guide. He prays to Mary on Dante's behalf and points him toward the Beatific Vision.
aliases: the one who drank his beauty

glossary.gloss: The prayerful, loving gazing on God that Bernard practiced even on earth; the path by which the soul rises toward the vision of God.
Originally the red war-banner of the French kings; Dante turns it into a 'war-banner of peace,' the brightest center of the Rose where Mary sits surrounded by reveling angels.

The mother of Christ, Queen of Heaven, who sits enthroned at the height of the Celestial Rose. In the final cantos all the blessed turn to her, the angel Gabriel sings 'Ave Maria,' and Bernard prays to her to win Dante the Beatific Vision.
aliases: the face that most of all resembles Christ

glossary.gloss: Latin for 'Hail Mary, full of grace,' the angel Gabriel's greeting at the Annunciation; sung again before Mary's throne in the Rose, with the whole court answering.
The archangel Gabriel, who bore 'the palm' to Mary at the Annunciation; in Canto XXXII he gazes into her eyes with such love he seems made of fire.
aliases: the one who bore the palm

glossary.gloss: The first woman, who first opened the wound of sin that Mary later healed; she sits in the Rose at Mary's feet, beneath her.
aliases: the one who first opened it and pierced

glossary.gloss: The biblical matriarch, wife of Abraham, among the Hebrew women seated in descending grades of the Rose.
The biblical matriarch, wife of Isaac, among the Hebrew women in the Rose.
The biblical heroine who slew Holofernes to save her people, seated among the Hebrew women of the Rose.
King David, the psalmist who, grieving his sin, prayed 'Miserere' (Have mercy); his great-grandmother (Ruth) is named among the women of the Rose.
The holy women of the Old Testament, seated in the Rose so as to form the wall dividing those who believed in Christ to come from those who looked back to Christ already come.
The great forerunner of Christ, who endured the desert and martyrdom and then waited two years in Limbo; he sits in the Rose directly opposite the Virgin Mary, dividing the other half of the flower.
Saint Benedict, founder of Western monasticism, seated beneath John the Baptist among the dividing saints of the Rose.
Jacob and Esau, who (Scripture says) struggled in Rebecca's womb; Bernard cites them to show God's grace is given freely, in differing measure, before any merit.
The souls of children who died before they could make any real choice; they are placed in the Rose by another's grace, under set terms, and their voices are still childlike.
aliases: spirits all absolved and freed before they ever made a real choice

glossary.gloss: Adam and Saint Peter, seated highest in the Rose nearest Mary, called the two roots from which the Rose has grown: Adam (the father of fallen humanity) and Peter (the father of the Church).
aliases: the two roots from which this Rose has grown

glossary.term: the ancient father of Holy Church
glossary.gloss: Saint Peter, to whose keeping Christ entrusted the keys of the Church; he sits at Mary's right hand in the Rose, opposite Anna.

glossary.term: he who saw, before he came to die
glossary.gloss: Saint John the Evangelist, author of Revelation, who foresaw the hard days of the Church (the Bride); he sits next to Peter in the Rose.

glossary.term: that leader under whom there lived on manna
glossary.gloss: Moses, who led the ungrateful, stiff-necked Israelites through the desert, where they were fed on manna; he sits among the highest in the Rose.
Saint Anne, the mother of the Virgin Mary, seated across from Peter in the Rose, gazing so contentedly on her daughter that she never stirs her eyes while singing Hosanna.
God, the first and supreme Love, toward whom Bernard finally turns Dante's eyes for the Beatific Vision.
An old word for a prayer; Bernard's 'holy orison' is his great prayer to the Virgin Mary that opens the final canto.
The direct sight of God himself, the goal of the whole journey, granted to Dante at the climax of Canto XXXIII; a vision so great that speech and memory fail before it.
God, the supreme uncreated Light into which Dante gazes at the end, dwelling in himself alone, knowing and loving himself; the source and end of all being.
aliases: the High Light that is true of itself

glossary.gloss: Philosophical terms: 'substance' is what a thing is in itself, 'accident' a quality it merely happens to have. Dante sees them all bound together as one in the divine Light.
aliases: substance and accident and how they act

glossary.gloss: The ship of Jason and the Argonauts, the first ship ever built; its shadow made the sea-god Neptune marvel. Dante measures the vastness of his forgetting against the twenty-five centuries since that voyage.
The prophecies the ancient Sibyl wrote on leaves, which scattered on the wind and were lost; Dante's image for how the details of his vision slip from memory.
The vision of the Trinity at the very end: three circles of three colors but one size, the first mirrored by the second and the third breathed equally from both (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit).
In the second circle of the Trinity (the Son), Dante glimpses a human image painted within the divine Light, the mystery of Christ's incarnation, which draws all his sight.
A mathematician who strains to 'square the circle' and cannot find the principle; Dante's image for his own helplessness before the mystery of how the human image fits within the divine circle.

glossary.term: the Love that moves the sun and the other stars
glossary.gloss: God, the divine Love that moves all creation; the final line of the whole poem, naming the power that now turns Dante's own desire and will in perfect harmony.
The mountain-island in the southern hemisphere where saved souls cleanse themselves of their sins before they can rise to heaven. It is the 'second kingdom' of the poem, between Hell and Paradise.
In the myth Dante alludes to, the nine daughters of Pierus challenged the Muses to a singing contest, lost, and were turned into magpies as punishment.
Adam and Eve, the first humans, who in Dante's scheme once lived on this mountain in the Garden of Eden before the Fall.
Cato of Utica, the grave guardian of the shore of Purgatory; see Cato.
Virgil, the Roman poet who is Dante's guide through Hell and Purgatory; called variously his Leader, Guide, Master, and Poet.
The Virgin Mary (or, by extension, the heavenly ladies who set Dante's journey in motion); here the 'Lady from heaven' whose prayers sent Virgil to rescue Dante.
The Last Judgment, when the saved will be reunited with their bodies, which will 'shine bright'; Cato's body will be glorified then.
The seven terraces of Mount Purgatory, one for each of the seven deadly sins, through which the souls climb to be purified.
The angel who guards the gate of Purgatory, one of the blessed spirits of Paradise; Dante must be cleansed before coming before him.
The goddess of the dawn in Roman myth; her 'cheeks' are the colors of the sunrise reddening over the sea.
Held by Dante to be the center of the inhabited world and exactly opposite Mount Purgatory on the globe, so that it is noon there when dawn breaks here.
The great river of India, marking the eastern edge of the world in Dante's geography; night is pictured rising from there.
The celestial boatman who ferries saved souls from the mouth of the Tiber across the sea to the shore of Purgatory, propelled only by his own wings.
Latin opening of Psalm 114, 'When Israel went out of Egypt' — sung by the arriving souls; it figures the soul's deliverance from the bondage of sin.
aliases: When Israel went out of Egypt

glossary.gloss: The constellation/zodiac sign whose place in the sky the rising sun has just driven down, a way of marking the hour of morning.
The souls in Purgatory, who appear as solid bodies but cannot be embraced because they are pure spirit; Dante's hands pass through Casella three times.
aliases: empty shadows — solid only to the eye

glossary.gloss: A musician and friend of Dante from Florence, now a saved soul. He sings one of Dante's own love poems so sweetly that everyone forgets the climb until Cato rebukes them.
The river of Rome; saved souls gather at its mouth to be ferried to Purgatory, a sign that they die within the Church.

glossary.term: Love that discourses in my mind
glossary.gloss: The opening line of one of Dante's own love poems (a canzone from his Convivio), which Casella sets to music and sings on the shore.
Cato again, who rebukes the souls for lingering over Casella's song instead of hurrying to begin their purification.
The southern Italian port where Virgil died; his body was later moved to Naples.
The Italian city where Virgil's body is buried, as he tells Dante to explain why he casts no shadow.
The Christian doctrine of the Trinity — one God in three Persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) — whose workings, Virgil says, human reason cannot fully trace.
The great Greek philosopher (384–322 BC); Virgil names him among the noble pagans in Limbo who longed in vain for the knowledge faith gives.
A town on the Ligurian coast; with Turbia it marks the ends of a notoriously rough, broken stretch of cliffs — yet an easy stair next to the slope Dante must climb.
A town near the French-Italian border (La Turbie); paired with Lerici to name the wildest coastal terrain, far easier than Dante's climb.

King of Sicily (1232–66), illegitimate son of Emperor Frederick II and grandson of Empress Constance. Excommunicated and killed at Benevento, he tells Dante he repented at the last moment and was saved despite the Church's curse.
Constance of Sicily (1154–1198), grandmother of Manfred and mother of Emperor Frederick II. (Manfred's own daughter Constance is the 'good Constance' he asks Dante to reassure.)
The island kingdom Manfred ruled; he refers to his royal descendants as 'the pride of Sicily and of Aragon.'
The Spanish kingdom into which Manfred's daughter married; her sons were rulers of Sicily and Aragon.
The Archbishop of Cosenza, sent by Pope Clement IV to pursue Manfred; he had Manfred's excommunicate bones dug up and cast out beyond the kingdom's border.
Pope Clement IV (reigned 1265–68), the enemy of Manfred who blessed the campaign against him.
The site of the 1266 battle where Manfred was killed; his soldiers heaped stones over his grave near the bridge there.
A river (the Liri/Garigliano) marking the edge of Manfred's kingdom, where his bones were finally cast out with extinguished candles, the ritual of excommunication.
The Roman Catholic Church; those who die excommunicate ('cut off from Holy Church') must wait outside Purgatory thirty times the years of their defiance, unless prayers shorten it.

Souls who repented only at the very end of life — the excommunicate (Manfred), the lazy (Belacqua), the violently slain, and the negligent princes — who must wait in Ante-Purgatory before they may begin to climb.
A steep hilltop town in central Italy, named as a hard climb that is still easy next to the cleft Dante must scale.
A coastal town reached by a steep descent, named with San Leo and Bismantova as difficult but still passable on foot.
A high, sheer rock formation in the Apennines, named as a steep but climbable height, unlike Dante's path which requires 'flying.'
The twin stars of the constellation Gemini; Virgil uses them to explain the sun's path. If the sun were in Gemini rather than Aries, it would ride even higher toward the pole.
The hill of Jerusalem; Virgil tells Dante to imagine Zion and Mount Purgatory as antipodes sharing one horizon but in opposite hemispheres, to grasp why the sun stands to the north here.
The mid-circle of the sky's daily motion, which always lies between the sun and winter; Dante grasps that from Purgatory it appears displaced toward the north.
The people of ancient Israel, who saw the celestial equator toward the south ('the warm lands'), opposite to how it appears from Purgatory in the southern hemisphere.

A lazy Florentine (a lute-maker known to Dante) found slumped behind a rock among the spiritually slothful. Famous for putting off his good 'sighs' until the end, he must now wait outside as long as he delayed in life.
Spiritual laziness or negligence; the sin of those, like Belacqua, who delayed repentance, here personified as a figure so idle she could be Belacqua's sister.

glossary.term: angel of God who sits up at the gate
glossary.gloss: The gatekeeper angel of Purgatory proper; Belacqua says this angel will not yet let him pass on to the cleansing terraces until his waiting time is served.
The far western edge of the known world; Dante marks the hour by saying night's foot is already on Morocco as noon comes to Purgatory.
Latin opening of Psalm 51, 'Have mercy on me,' the great penitential psalm sung by the souls of the violently slain as they approach.
A band of souls in Ante-Purgatory who were killed by violence and repented only at the last breath, forgiving their killers as they died; they beg for prayers from the living.
The people of Padua (said to be founded by the Trojan Antenor); Jacopo del Cassero was murdered in their territory, where he felt safest.
Azzo VIII of Este, marquis of Ferrara, who out of hatred ordered the assassination of Jacopo del Cassero.
A village near Padua; Jacopo says that had he fled toward the Mira instead, he might have escaped his killers.
The marshy place near the Venetian lagoon where Jacopo del Cassero was caught and killed, bleeding out in the reeds.

Buonconte da Montefeltro, a Ghibelline captain killed at the battle of Campaldino (1289). He tells how he died with Mary's name on his lips, was saved for a single tear, and his body was swept away by the flooded Archiano river so it was never found.
The mountain district of which Buonconte's family were lords; he names it as his origin.
Buonconte's wife, who no longer prays for him; he laments that no one cares for his soul.
The battlefield (1289) where Buonconte died; Dante himself fought there. Buonconte's body was carried far from it and never buried.
A mountain torrent in the Casentino that swept up Buonconte's dead body and carried it into the Arno, undoing the cross his arms had made.
The monastery of Camaldoli in the Apennines, above which the Archiano river rises.

glossary.term: the Angel of God took me
glossary.gloss: The angel that claims Buonconte's soul, while a devil from hell, cheated of him by one repentant tear, vents his rage on the corpse by raising a storm.
A mountain ridge in Tuscany; the devil's storm fills the valley with fog from Pratomagno to the great Apennine ridge.
A gentle Sienese woman, 'La Pia de' Tolomei,' murdered in the wild Maremma (it is hinted by her own husband). Her brief, famous lines ask only to be remembered.
The Tuscan city; La Pia says 'Siena made me' (it was her birthplace), and the city figures throughout these cantos as the home of Provenzano Salvani.
A dice game; Dante opens Canto 6 by comparing himself, mobbed by souls begging for prayers, to the winner at dice surrounded by a pressing crowd.
Benincasa da Laterina, a judge of Arezzo killed by the bandit Ghino di Tacco; one of the violently slain souls Dante glimpses.
A notorious outlaw of Dante's day who murdered the judge from Arezzo.
A young Tuscan nobleman of the Conti Guidi, slain in a feud; among the violently dead praying for help.
Gano (Cione) degli Scornigiani of Pisa, whose death made his father, the good Marzucco, show heroic restraint by forgiving the killer.
Marzucco degli Scornigiani of Pisa, praised for the saintly self-mastery he showed at the murder of his son.
Count Orso degli Alberti, killed by a kinsman in a family feud; one of the slain souls Dante sees.
A favorite of King Philip III of France, brought down by court intrigue and hanged. Dante warns the Lady of Brabant, whom he blames, to mend her ways before she dies.
Mary of Brabant, queen of France, accused of plotting the downfall of Pierre de la Brosse; Dante warns her to repent lest she end among the damned.
Virgil, addressed by Dante as 'my light' as he questions whether prayer can really change a decree of heaven, citing Virgil's own Aeneid.
Sordello, the proud, aloof spirit who watches the poets like a resting lion before revealing himself; see Sordello.

A famous 13th-century Mantuan troubadour poet. He embraces Virgil simply because they share a homeland — which sparks Dante's furious lament over a divided, warring Italy. Sordello becomes their guide to the Valley of Princes.
Dante's bitter apostrophe to a divided, lordless Italy — 'a ship without a pilot,' 'a brothel' — torn by civil war while its rightful ruler, the Emperor, neglects it.
Albert I of Habsburg, Holy Roman Emperor (1298–1308), whom Dante reproaches for abandoning Italy by never coming to rule it, lured instead by lands in the north.
Two feuding noble families of northern Italy whose strife Dante holds up as a symbol of the country's ruin; later made famous by Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet.
Two rival families of Orvieto, named with the Montagues and Capulets as examples of the factional violence tearing Italy apart.
A county in the Sienese Maremma, ruined by feud and lawlessness; Dante names it ironically when calling the Emperor to see how 'safe' his lands have become.
A Roman who opposed Julius Caesar; Dante says every petty peasant in faction-ridden Italy now plays the would-be 'Marcellus,' the self-important partisan.
The two famous law-giving cities of ancient Greece; Dante says their celebrated good order looks feeble next to the (ironically) ever-changing 'wisdom' of Florence.
The emperor Augustus (Octavian), under whose reign Virgil lived and died; Virgil says his bones were buried by Octavian's order.
The three theological virtues — faith, hope, and charity (love); Virgil dwells in Limbo with the virtuous pagans who never knew these, though they practiced the four natural virtues.
Unbaptized infants who died before they could be cleansed of original sin; they dwell with Virgil in Limbo.
A fragrant flowered hollow on the mountainside where the souls of negligent rulers, who put worldly affairs before their salvation, gather and sing until they may begin to climb.
Latin opening of the hymn 'Hail, Queen' (to the Virgin Mary), sung by the negligent rulers in the Valley of Princes.
Ottokar II, king of Bohemia (d. 1278), a worthy ruler who comforts Rudolph in the valley despite having been his enemy in life; his land lies where the Moldau flows to the Elbe.
The river (Vltava) of Bohemia, which carries its waters to the Elbe and so to the sea; used to locate Ottokar's kingdom.
The great central-European river into which the Moldau flows; named to place Ottokar's realm of Bohemia.
Wenceslaus II of Bohemia, Ottokar's son, condemned by Dante as a slothful, pleasure-loving king, lesser than his bearded father.
Philip III of France, who 'died in flight, deflowering the lily' (disgracing the French royal arms); he beats his breast in repentance in the valley.
Philip IV ('the Fair') of France, whom Dante despises; the kings beside him are his father (Philip III) and father-in-law (Henry of Navarre), grieving over his corrupt life.
Pedro III, king of Aragon, the 'sturdy' soul with the strong nose who sang in the valley; he 'wore the cord of every worth,' meaning he had every kingly virtue.
Two of Pedro III of Aragon's sons (Frederick of Sicily and James of Aragon), who inherited his kingdoms but not his goodness.
Margaret of Provence, queen of France; named with Beatrice as the wives whose husbands' worth was less than that of Pedro III, whom Constance still boasts of.
Henry III of England, called 'the king of the simple life,' who sits alone in the valley; Dante says his heirs (his son Edward I) turned out better than himself.
William VII, marquis of Montferrat, the lowest soul in the valley; his war with Alessandria led to his capture and death, bringing grief to Montferrat and the Canavese.
The Lombard city whose war against William of Montferrat brought him to ruin.
The marquisate of Montferrat in Piedmont, which weeps for the captured William along with the neighboring Canavese.
A district of Piedmont near Montferrat, named as mourning the fate of William the Marquis.
Latin opening of the evening hymn 'Te lucis ante terminum' ('Before the ending of the light'), sung by the souls in the valley at nightfall, asking God's protection against the dark and the tempter.

glossary.term: two angels with two flaming swords
glossary.gloss: Two green-robed angels sent down from Mary to guard the Valley of Princes against the serpent each night; their swords are broken short, mercy outweighing judgment.
The snake that creeps into the valley each evening, recalling the serpent that tempted Eve; the guardian angels drive it off. It symbolizes recurring temptation.
Nino Visconti of Pisa, a judge (ruler) of the district of Gallura in Sardinia and a friend of Dante. Glad to be found among the saved, he laments that his widow has remarried.
Currado Malaspina, a noble of the Lunigiana whom Nino calls over; he praises his family's honor and foretells Dante's exile and welcome among the Malaspina. (See Currado Malaspina.)
The young daughter of Judge Nino Visconti; he asks Dante to have her pray for him 'where the innocent are heard.'

The serpent emblem on the coat of arms of the Visconti of Milan; Nino bitterly says his widow's new husband (a Milanese Visconti) will not honor her grave as his own emblem, the Gallura Cock, would have.
The rooster on the coat of arms of Nino Visconti, judge of Gallura in Sardinia; he contrasts it proudly with the Milanese Viper.
The people of Milan, ruled by the Visconti whose viper emblem Nino disdains; his widow's new husband leads them to war.
Three bright stars that have risen in the south where the four morning stars (the cardinal virtues) had set; these three stand for the three theological virtues — faith, hope, charity.
The valley of the Magra river in the Lunigiana, the homeland of the Malaspina family; Currado asks for news of it.

A descendant of the older Currado, of the noble Malaspina family of the Lunigiana. He prophesies that within seven years Dante will learn the family's generosity firsthand (a hint of Dante's exile and their hospitality).
In myth the mortal husband of Aurora (the dawn); Dante opens Canto 9 by describing Aurora, 'the mistress of old Tithonus,' brightening at the eastern rail.
The constellation Scorpio (the 'cold creature whose tail comes lashing down'), whose shape gleams in the gems on the dawn's forehead, marking the hour.
The swallow whose plaintive song near dawn recalls the myth of Procne, turned into a bird after a family tragedy; Dante sets the hour of his prophetic dream by it.
The golden eagle in Dante's dream that snatches him up to the sphere of fire, paralleling the myth of Ganymede; it foreshadows St. Lucia carrying him up the mountain.
In myth, the beautiful Trojan youth seized by Jove's eagle and carried up to Olympus to serve the gods; Dante dreams of being snatched up like him.
Olympus, the council of the gods, to which Ganymede was carried up by the eagle in the myth Dante's dream echoes.
The island where the goddess Thetis hid her son Achilles (disguised as a girl) to keep him from the Trojan War, until the Greeks drew him out to fight.
The Achaeans who fought at Troy; they later found Achilles on Scyros and led him to the war.

The three colored stairs before the gate of Purgatory: white marble (contrition, the honest mirror of self), cracked dark stone (confession, the broken heart), and flaming red porphyry (satisfaction, the love that pays for sin).
The gatekeeper of Purgatory proper, seated on the threshold with a blinding sword. He cuts seven P's on Dante's brow, draws two keys, and admits him with the warning not to look back.
A hard, deep-red stone; the third step before the gate is likened to porphyry 'flaming red as blood,' symbolizing the ardent love of true satisfaction for sin.
The seven letters P (for Latin 'peccatum,' sin) that the angel carves into Dante's forehead — one for each deadly sin — to be erased one by one as he climbs the seven terraces.

The gold and silver keys, given to the angel by St. Peter, with which he unlocks the gate of Purgatory; the silver takes skill and judgment, the gold is more precious — together they stand for the Church's power to absolve.
