The treasury of ancient Rome on the Tarpeian/Capitoline hill; Dante compares the loud grinding of Purgatory's gate to the roar when Caesar forced it open over the protests of Metellus.
The Roman tribune who tried to stop Julius Caesar from seizing the public treasury on the Tarpeian rock; the gate's grinding sound recalls that famous clamor.
Latin opening of the ancient hymn of praise 'We praise you, O God,' which Dante hears sung as the gate of Purgatory swings open behind him.
The first of the seven terraces of Purgatory proper, where the souls of the proud are bent double under crushing stones; here Dante meets Omberto, Oderisi, and hears of Provenzano Salvani.
A famous ancient Greek sculptor; the carvings on the terrace of pride are so lifelike that they would shame both Polyclitus and Nature herself.
The angel Gabriel's greeting 'Ave' (Hail) to Mary at the Annunciation, carved so vividly into the marble that the figure seems to speak it; it is an exemplar of humility against pride.
Latin for 'Behold the handmaid of God,' Mary's humble reply to the angel at the Annunciation, carved beside Gabriel as the supreme image of humility on the terrace of pride.
The Ark of the Covenant; a carving shows the cart and oxen drawing it, and Uzzah struck dead for touching it — a warning against presuming to an 'office not given' to one.
King David, who danced humbly before the Ark of the Covenant with his robe hitched up, 'both more and less than king' — an exemplar of humility carved on the terrace.
King David's wife (daughter of Saul), shown in the carving looking down in scornful pride as David dances humbly before the Ark — a figure of haughtiness.

The Roman emperor Trajan, shown in a carved scene halting his army to give justice to a poor widow whose son was killed; his humble goodness later (by legend) won his salvation through the prayers of Pope Gregory.

The grieving widow in the Trajan carving who demands justice for her murdered son and persuades the emperor to grant it before he rides to war; an exemplar of righteous appeal answered by humble justice.
Dante's image for the redeemed soul: human beings are 'worms' born to become the butterfly that flies up to God's justice; he reproaches the proud for forgetting this.
Those Dante addresses on the terrace of pride — sinners 'sick in the eye of the mind' who trust in things that carry them backward; pride is the root of all sin.
The Lord's Prayer, which the souls on the terrace of pride recite in an expanded, paraphrased form as they circle bent under their stones — a fitting prayer of humility for the once-proud.
Satan, the devil who tempts mankind; the souls pray in the Lord's Prayer to be delivered from him — though they add the petition is now only for the living, not themselves.
Omberto Aldobrandeschi, a Tuscan nobleman so puffed up by his ancient lineage that his contempt for others got him killed and ruined his whole family; now he carries the stone of pride.
The great Tuscan lord, father of Omberto, of the proud Aldobrandeschi line whose nobility fed Omberto's fatal arrogance.
The Aldobrandeschi stronghold in the Sienese countryside where Omberto was killed; 'every child in Campagnatico' knows the story.
The people of Siena, who know how Omberto's pride brought about his death.
Oderisi of Gubbio, a celebrated manuscript illuminator. On the terrace of pride he confesses his old hunger for artistic fame and preaches the emptiness of worldly glory, citing how reputations fade.
The Umbrian town that was the home and pride of the illuminator Oderisi.
The art of decorating manuscripts with painted miniatures and ornament ('illumination'), the craft for which Oderisi was famous, especially as practiced in Paris.
A manuscript illuminator of Bologna whose work, Oderisi humbly admits, now outshines his own — an example of how fame passes from one master to the next.
The Florentine painter Cimabue, who thought himself supreme in his art until Giotto eclipsed him — Oderisi's example of how artistic fame fades.
The great Florentine painter who surpassed Cimabue; cited by Oderisi to show how quickly one famous artist replaces another.

glossary.term: one Guido has taken from the other
glossary.gloss: A reference to two poets named Guido — Guido Cavalcanti eclipsing Guido Guinizelli in fame — and a hint that a third (Dante himself) may surpass them both; an example of passing glory.

The powerful Ghibelline lord of Siena who tried to bring all the city under his rule. He is on the terrace of pride; his early entry was won by a single act of humility — begging in the public square to ransom a friend.
The great public square of Siena, where the proud Provenzano Salvani once set himself to beg, swallowing all shame, to ransom a friend from Charles's prison — the humbling act that freed him.
The prison of Charles of Anjou, where Provenzano Salvani's friend was held for ransom; to free him, Provenzano debased himself by begging.
An Italian (literally a man of Latium/Italy); Omberto identifies himself as 'a Latian, born of a great Tuscan.'
The ancient Romans / Italians; Sordello hails Virgil as 'glory of the Latins,' the poet through whom the Latin (Italian) tongue showed all it could do.

In Greek myth, the son of Agamemnon, famous for his selfless friendship with Pylades; each tried to die in the other's place. His name is one of the disembodied voices on the terrace of envy, held up as an example of generous love.

The sin purged on this second terrace of Purgatory, where souls who took pleasure in others' losses have their eyes sewn shut with wire. Dante treats it as love gone wrong: grieving at another's good.
The stairway and angel that mark the climb from one terrace of Purgatory to the next, where a sin is forgiven and a mark wiped from the climber's brow.

A noblewoman of Siena who rejoiced at the defeat and death of her own townsmen at the battle of Colle. She tells Dante her story on the terrace of the envious. Her name puns on the Italian for 'wise' (savia), which she says she was not.
Colle di Val d'Elsa, where the Sienese army was routed in 1269. Sapia watched her own city's troops flee and felt unmatched joy at their ruin.
A holy comb-seller of Siena whose prayers, Sapia says, shortened her time of waiting before she could enter Purgatory.
A seaport the Sienese vainly hoped would make their city rich; Sapia mocks her townsmen's false hopes in it.
An underground stream the Sienese spent fortunes searching for beneath their city. Sapia jeers at the hunt for it as another of her people's empty hopes.
The region of central Italy that includes Florence and Siena, Dante's homeland. Souls and shades repeatedly ask after news of it.
The mountain in the Apennines where the river Arno rises. Dante names it instead of naming the Arno outright.
A nobleman of Romagna who confesses on the terrace of the envious that his blood once burned with envy. He delivers a long lament for the ruined virtue of the great families of Romagna.
Rinieri da Calboli, a nobleman of Forlì sitting beside Guido del Duca. Guido names him the last honor of the decayed house of Calboli.
A noble house of Romagna; Guido del Duca mourns that no descendant since Rinieri has lived up to its name.
A town of Romagna whose noble families have fled corruption; Guido del Duca asks why it does not flee too.
A town of Romagna; Guido praises it for having no more sons to carry on a degenerate line.
In Greek myth, a girl turned to stone for her envy of her sister's love. Her name is the second thunderous example of envy punished, called out from the air.
The devil, Satan, whose hook draws human souls in when they swallow the bait of earthly goods. Virgil names him as the tempter behind envy.
Latin, 'Blessed are the merciful' (from the Beatitudes), sung by the angel as Dante leaves the terrace of envy; mercy is the virtue opposed to envy.
The mild ruler of ancient Athens. In Dante's vision he is an example of gentleness: when his wife demands revenge on a youth who kissed their daughter, he refuses to harm one who loves them.
The Persian king of the Book of Esther. He appears in Dante's vision of meekness opposed to wrath, alongside Esther and Mordecai.
The Jewish queen of Persia who, with Mordecai, foiled Haman's plot; part of Dante's vision of gentleness on the terrace of the wrathful.
The just man of the Book of Esther, Esther's kinsman, shown in Dante's vision as an example against anger.
The sin purged on the terrace of black smoke, where the angry are wrapped in choking darkness. Examples of gentleness teach the virtue that opposes it.
Latin, 'Lamb of God,' the prayer the souls in the smoke chant in perfect concord as they loosen the knot of wrath.

A wise Lombard courtier who, on the terrace of wrath, explains free will to Dante and argues that the world's corruption comes from bad leadership, not the stars. He frames it with the image of Rome's 'two suns.'
The doctrine, central to Marco Lombardo's speech, that humans are free to choose good or evil and so are responsible for the world's state; the heavens may incline but do not compel.

Marco Lombardo's image for the proper order of Rome: the Empire (worldly power) and the Church (spiritual power) as two separate lights. He laments that the Church has put out the Empire and seized the sword along with the crook.
God, the source of motion and of the new soul breathed into the unborn child; named in Statius's account of how the soul is formed.
One of three old men of Lombardy whom Marco Lombardo names as surviving examples of the old virtue, shaming the new age.
Gherardo da Camino, named by Marco Lombardo as a 'good Gherardo,' a remnant of the vanished age of virtue; his daughter was Gaia.
A Lombard nobleman named by Marco as another remnant of old courtesy, called 'the plain Lombard' in the French manner.
The priestly tribe of Israel, barred from inheriting land. Dante cites 'the sons of Levi' to show why the Church should hold no worldly power.
The inner faculty Dante addresses directly, which can seize a person so wholly that the outer senses go unheard; it is moved by a light formed in heaven.
Latin, 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (from the Beatitudes), sung by the angel as Dante leaves the terrace of wrath.
A river of Thebes; Dante compares the racing slothful to the Theban crowds that thronged its banks in worship of Bacchus.
A river near Thebes, named with the Ismenus in the simile of nighttime crowds rushing to honor Bacchus.
A penitent on the terrace of sloth who served as abbot of San Zeno in Verona under Barbarossa; he foretells trouble for his monastery under a corrupt successor.
Emperor Frederick I 'Barbarossa,' who destroyed much of Milan; the Abbot of San Zeno held his post under his rule.
In Dante's dream, a stammering, deformed woman who becomes beautiful and seductive as he gazes at her; she stands for the false sweetness of greed, gluttony, and lust. A holy lady exposes her stench.
Greed for money and worldly goods, the sin purged on the fifth terrace, where souls lie face-down, bound, weeping 'My soul has clung to the dust.'

The penitent on the terrace of avarice who reveals he was once 'the successor of Peter.' He held the papacy barely a month and learned only then how worldly life is a lie. He refuses Dante's kneeling, saying they are fellow servants.
The niece of Pope Adrian V, a good woman who is all the family he says is left to him on earth, and whose prayers he hopes for.
Dante's emblem of avarice, the beast that seizes more prey than any other, driven by a bottomless hunger; he curses her and longs for the one who will drive her off.
A Roman general famous for choosing honest poverty over bribes; cited by Hugh Capet as an example of virtuous poverty, the opposite of avarice.
Saint Nicholas, who secretly gave gold to three poor maidens to save them from disgrace; named among the examples of generosity that rebuke avarice.

The founder of the Capetian dynasty of French kings, who speaks at length on the terrace of avarice. He calls himself the root of an 'evil plant' shadowing Christendom and condemns the crimes of his royal descendants.
The young Hohenstaufen heir executed by Charles of Anjou; Hugh Capet names him among Charles's victims.
The lily emblem of the French royal house; Hugh Capet foresees it entering Anagni, where the French outraged Pope Boniface VIII ('Christ made captive in his own Vicar').
The Italian town where agents of the French king seized and humiliated Pope Boniface VIII in 1303; Hugh Capet sees in it a fresh crucifixion of Christ in his Vicar.
A king who murdered his own kinsman out of lust for gold; the avaricious recall him by night as an example of greed's crimes.
The king whose greedy wish turned all he touched to gold; named by the avaricious souls as a laughable warning.
The Israelite who stole forbidden spoils and was destroyed by Joshua's wrath; cited by the avaricious as an example of theft.
With her husband Ananias, struck dead in Acts for lying about money kept back from the apostles; named among the avaricious souls' examples.
A royal official driven off by heavenly horsemen when he tried to plunder the Temple in Jerusalem; the avaricious 'praise the hooves' that trampled him.
The king who murdered Polydorus for his gold; named in infamy by the avaricious souls.
The Roman triumvir notorious for greed, said to have had molten gold poured down his throat; the avaricious mockingly ask him 'what does gold taste like?'
The floating island that was made stable so Latona could give birth there; Dante compares the shaking mountain to it, saying Delos shook less.
The mother of Apollo and Diana ('the two eyes of heaven'), who bore them on Delos; named in the simile for the trembling mountain.

The Roman poet (author of the Thebaid and the unfinished Achilleid) whose soul Dante meets on the terrace of avarice, freed at last to rise. He reveals he was a secret Christian, converted by reading Virgil, and joins Dante and Virgil for the rest of Purgatory.
One of the three Fates, who loads the distaff with the thread of each life; Virgil names her in explaining that Statius's thread of life is fully spun while Dante's is not.
The Fate who spins the thread of life; when she has no more thread, the soul leaves the body. Named by Statius in his account of the soul.
The city Statius is here said to come from (a medieval error confusing him with another Statius); he says Rome drew him from Toulouse and crowned him with the myrtle.
Virgil's epic of Aeneas, which Statius calls the 'mother and nurse' of his own poetry and the divine flame that made him a poet.
The Roman satirist who, dying, came down to Limbo and there told Virgil of Statius's love for him, kindling Virgil's affection in return.
The mother of Oedipus; her two sons, Eteocles and Polynices, killed each other warring over Thebes, the 'twofold grief' Statius sang of.
The Muse of history, named as the Muse Statius invoked in writing the Thebaid; Virgil uses her to mark that Statius wrote before his conversion.
Saint Peter, the fisherman-apostle; Virgil asks what light led Statius to 'set his sails to follow the Fisherman,' that is, to become a Christian.
The Roman emperor who persecuted Christians; Statius lived through it, secretly mourning with the persecuted believers.
A Roman comic playwright; Statius asks Virgil whether he and other classical poets are damned and in which circle of Hell.
An early Roman comic poet, named among the classical writers Statius asks after.
The Roman comic playwright, named among the poets Statius inquires about.
A Roman writer named among the classical authors Statius asks Virgil about.
The Roman satirist, named by Virgil as one of the poets dwelling with him in Limbo.
The Greek tragic playwright, named among the Greek poets who dwell with Virgil in Limbo.
A Greek tragic poet named among the classical Greeks in Limbo.
A Greek lyric poet, named among the laurel-crowned Greeks in Limbo.
A Greek tragic poet, named among the Greeks dwelling with Virgil in Limbo.
A daughter of Oedipus and a figure of Statius's Thebaid; named among the Theban characters Statius may see in Limbo.
A figure from the Theban legend, named among the women of Statius's poems present in Limbo.
The wife of Polynices in the Theban story; named among the women of Statius's poems in Limbo.
A daughter of Oedipus, sister of Antigone, 'mournful as she ever was,' named among the Theban figures in Limbo.
The sea-nymph mother of Achilles, a figure of Statius's Achilleid, named among those in Limbo.
John the Baptist, who fed on honey and locusts in the wilderness; named as a model of abstinence on the terrace of gluttony.
The sin purged on the sixth terrace, where the greedy-mouthed are starved gaunt before tantalizing fruit and water; examples of temperance hang in the trees.
In Greek myth, a man cursed with insatiable hunger who consumed himself; Dante compares the starved gluttons to him, saying even he was not so wasted.
The Latin/Italian word for 'man'; medieval lore held that a human face spells out OMO (the eyes as O's, the brow and nose as M). On the starved faces of the gluttons the M stands out plainly.

Forese Donati, Dante's friend and kinsman by marriage, met among the gluttons. So wasted Dante knows him only by his voice, he praises his widow Nella and foretells trouble for the shameless women of Florence.
The devout widow of Forese Donati, whose tears and prayers (Forese says) raised him so quickly up the mountain; he calls her his 'little widow.'
A wild mountain region of Sardinia known for immodest women; Forese uses it twice to shame the bare-breasted women of Florence as worse than savages.
Father of Iris the rainbow; Statius mentions that no 'daughter of Thaumas' (no rainbow) appears above the lowest steps of the mountain.
The angel-gatekeeper who sets his feet at the top of the three steps; Statius marks this as the upper limit of all earthly weather and disturbance.
The woman at the well in John's Gospel who asked Christ for living water; Dante invokes her thirst as an image of his own longing to understand.
The biblical judge who dismissed the soldiers who drank greedily, keeping only the temperate; cited at the gluttons' tree.
The land Gideon marched against; named in the example of soldiers tested by how they drank.
Here a poetic name for Heaven, the highest realm where the blessed dwell, not the mountain of the Greek gods.
Bonagiunta degli Orbicciani of Lucca, an older Italian poet among the gluttons; he praises Dante's 'sweet new style' and admits his own circle never matched it.
French city; the gluttonous pope referred to (Martin IV) came from near Tours and was famous for gorging on eels from Lake Bolsena drowned in Vernaccia wine.
An Italian lake whose eels were a delicacy; named to mark the gluttony of Pope Martin IV.
A strong sweet white wine; the gluttonous pope was said to drown Bolsena's eels in it before eating them.
A Tuscan nobleman of the Ubaldini family, here among the gluttons, gnawing at empty air in his hunger.
Marchese degli Argogliosi of Forlì, a nobleman remembered as a heavy drinker who was never satisfied; now among the gluttons.
A young woman of Lucca whom Bonagiunta foretells; she will one day make Dante look kindly on the city others scorn.
The 'dolce stil novo,' the refined Italian love poetry pioneered by Dante and his friends, which follows the inward dictation of Love; Bonagiunta names it as what set Dante apart from earlier poets.

glossary.term: Ladies who have intelligence of love
glossary.gloss: The opening line of a famous canzone from Dante's youthful 'Vita Nuova,' cited as the breakthrough poem of the sweet new style.
Jacopo da Lentini, a Sicilian poet called 'the Notary,' grouped with Guittone and Bonagiunta as forerunners who fell short of Dante's new style.
Guittone d'Arezzo, a leading earlier Italian poet; both Bonagiunta and Guinizelli cite him as an overpraised predecessor surpassed by the new style.

glossary.term: the cursed ones formed out of the cloud
glossary.gloss: The Centaurs, born of Ixion and a cloud, who got drunk at a wedding and battled Theseus and the Lapiths; an example of riot bred by gluttony.
The zodiac sign the Bull; Dante uses it with Scorpio to mark the time of day as the sun and night shift positions.
The zodiac sign the Scorpion, paired with Taurus to mark the hour in Dante's astronomical timekeeping.
Greek hero whose life was magically bound to a burning log; he wasted away as it burned. Statius cites him to show how a body can be consumed without eating.
Latin, 'God of supreme mercy,' a hymn for chastity sung by the souls in the wall of fire who purge the sin of lust.
Latin, 'I know not a man,' Mary's words at the Annunciation (Luke 1:34), cried by the lustful souls as a model of chastity.
The nymph Callisto, seduced and so driven by Diana from the woods; her name appears among the chaste souls' examples of lust punished.
The cleansing flame on the seventh and final terrace of Purgatory, where the lustful are purified; every soul, Dante included, must pass through it to reach the Earthly Paradise.
Used as a figure for someone parched in a hot land, to convey how desperately the burning souls thirst for Dante's answer.
The biblical cities destroyed for sin; the souls who sinned against nature cry these names against themselves as they pass.
Queen of Crete who lusted after a bull and hid inside a wooden cow to mate with it, bearing the Minotaur; the souls who indulged natural lust to excess cry her name in self-reproach.
Legendary cold northern mountains; Dante compares the two groups of lustful souls to cranes flying part toward this frozen region, part toward warm sands.
Bolognese poet hailed by Dante as the 'father' of the sweet new style and of all who wrote graceful love verse; he greets Dante warmly from within the fire of the lustful.
King in Greek legend whose grief over a child's death is the model for a sudden, overpowering emotion; Dante likens his rush of feeling at Guinizelli's name to that scene.
Giraut de Bornelh, a celebrated Provençal troubadour from near Limoges; Guinizelli says fools wrongly rank him above Arnaut Daniel.

Arnaut Daniel, the great Provençal troubadour whom Guinizelli calls the finest craftsman of the mother tongue; he answers Dante in his own Occitan, weeping yet hopeful as he returns to the refining fire.
The old language of southern France and the troubadours, in which Arnaut Daniel speaks his lines to Dante.
A river in Spain; used with the Ganges to mark, by the sun's position, the hour at which the day was ending as Dante reached the wall of fire.
The zodiac sign the Scales; named in the astronomical figure that fixes the time of evening over Spain.
Latin, 'Blessed are the pure in heart,' the beatitude (Matthew 5:8) sung by the angel at the wall of fire.
Lover in the tale of Pyramus and Thisbe; dying, he opened his eyes at her name, and his blood stained the white mulberry red. Dante's resolve melts the same way at the name of Beatrice.
The beloved of Pyramus in the classical tragedy; her name, spoken over the dying Pyramus, makes him look up one last time.
Latin, 'Come, blessed of my Father' (Matthew 25:34), sung from a brightness to welcome the souls past the fire toward the Earthly Paradise.
A name for Venus as the morning star; Dante marks the hour by her first light on the mountain before his dream of Leah.
The first wife of Jacob in Genesis; in Dante's dream she gathers flowers and stands for the active life, contrasted with her contemplative sister Rachel.
The Garden of Eden at the summit of Mount Purgatory, the 'divine forest' where humanity once lived innocent; Dante reaches it after the fire and finds Matilda, the mystic procession, and Beatrice.
The classical god of the winds; Dante recalls the sound of the pine wood at Chiassi when Aeolus looses the Sirocco, to describe the murmuring forest of Eden.
A warm wind from the south; in the simile of the pine forest at Chiassi it stirs the trees the way the steady air moves Eden's branches.
The pine forest on the Adriatic shore near Ravenna (Classe); its rustling in the wind is Dante's image for the sound of Eden's wood.
The lovely lady who walks alone gathering flowers in the Earthly Paradise; she explains the place, its winds and waters, and later leads Dante through Lethe and Eunoë.
Daughter of Ceres, carried off by Pluto while gathering flowers; Matilda's flower-gathering recalls the moment Proserpina, and the Spring, were lost.
The narrow strait between Sestos and Abydos, crossed by Xerxes' army and swum by Leander; Dante says he resents the little stream of Eden as Leander resented this barrier.
Youth who swam the Hellespont nightly to reach his beloved Hero, hating the water that divided them; Dante likens his own longing across Eden's stream to Leander's.
Town on the European shore of the Hellespont, opposite Abydos, between which Leander swam.
Town on the Asian shore of the Hellespont, opposite Sestos, in the tale of Leander and Hero.
Latin word from Psalm 92, 'You have delighted me'; Matilda points to this psalm as the key to understanding the joy of the Earthly Paradise.
God, who delights in himself and made humankind good, giving Eden as a pledge of eternal peace before the Fall.
The second sacred river of the Earthly Paradise; its waters restore the memory of every good deed. Dante must drink from it after Lethe to be made wholly ready for Heaven.
The classical poets' lost golden age of innocence and endless spring; Matilda suggests they were dreaming of this very place, Eden.
Latin, 'Blessed are they whose sins are covered' (Psalm 32), sung by Matilda as she moves upstream in the Earthly Paradise.
The Muses' mountain with its inspiring springs; Dante calls on it to help him describe the mystic procession.
The Muse of the heavens and of sacred song; Dante invokes her and her choir to help him put the holy procession into verse.
A Hebrew cry of praise; sung in the procession of the Earthly Paradise as the seven golden candlesticks advance.
A name for Diana the moon goddess (born on Delos); 'Delia in her ring' is the halo round the moon, paired with the rainbow as colors of the procession's seven banners.
In the mystic procession, twenty-four white-robed elders crowned with lilies, figuring the books of the Old Testament; they sing the praise of Mary.
The four six-winged, eye-covered beasts of the procession, drawn from Ezekiel and Revelation; they figure the four Gospels and surround the chariot.
The hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth; the eyes covering the four living creatures' wings are said to outdo even those of Argus.
Old Testament prophet whose vision of the four winged creatures coming from the north (Ezekiel 1) Dante cites as the source for the beasts in the procession.
The eagle-lion creature, gold above and white-and-red below, who draws the triumphal chariot; a 'twin-natured' being figuring Christ in his divine and human natures.
The two-wheeled triumphal car drawn by the Griffin at the center of the mystic procession; it figures the Church, and its later violent transformations symbolize the Church's corruption.
Scipio Africanus, the Roman general honored with grand triumphs; even his processions, says Dante, were poorer than the Griffin's chariot.
The chariot of the sun-god, which Phaethon drove off course and scorched the earth until Jove struck it down; even it would seem poor beside the Griffin's car.
At the chariot's right wheel, the three theological virtues dancing in a ring: red Charity, green Hope, and snow-white Faith.
At the chariot's left wheel, four ladies in purple figuring the four cardinal virtues, led by the one with three eyes (Prudence, who sees past, present, and future).
The seven golden candlesticks of the procession, likened to the unfailing stars of the highest heaven that guide souls as the Wain (Big Dipper) guides sailors.
aliases: Sevenfold Stars of the highest heaven

glossary.gloss: The constellation of the Great Bear or Big Dipper, used by sailors to steer; Dante contrasts the lower Wain with the higher 'sevenfold stars' that guide the soul.
Latin, 'Come, bride, from Lebanon' (Song of Songs), sung three times to herald Beatrice's arrival on the chariot.
Latin, 'at the voice of so great an elder'; describes the hundred angels rising over the chariot in answer to the elder's song as Beatrice appears.
Latin, 'Blessed are you who come' (from the welcome to Christ entering Jerusalem), cried by the angels as Beatrice arrives.
Latin, 'Oh give lilies with full hands,' a line borrowed from Virgil's Aeneid, sung by the angels scattering flowers at Beatrice's coming.
The olive, sacred to Minerva (Athena), goddess of wisdom; Beatrice appears crowned with olive, signaling wisdom, over her white veil.
Latin, 'In you, Lord, I have hoped' (Psalm 31), sung by the angels in pity for Dante as Beatrice rebukes him; they sing only as far as 'my feet.'
The sea-creatures whose song lured sailors to ruin; Beatrice warns Dante to be stronger another time when he hears the Sirens, meaning the deceptive pull of earthly pleasures.
Libya, the land of King Iarbas; the gale from there (the Sirocco) is the wind in the simile of the oak torn up, measuring how hard Dante lifted his chin.
Latin, 'You will sprinkle me' (Psalm 51, a cleansing rite), sung as Matilda draws Dante through the waters of Lethe.
The four cardinal virtues (here called Nymphs), who dance and lead Dante to Beatrice's eyes after his immersion in Lethe.
The three theological virtues, who 'see more deeply' and will sharpen Dante's sight to bear the joyful light in Beatrice's eyes.
A figure for Beatrice's green, shining eyes, into which Dante gazes; 'where Love once drew his weapons against you' recalls how he first loved her.

The towering, leafless tree in the Earthly Paradise to which the Griffin binds the chariot; figuring God's justice, the tree of knowledge, and Roman imperial authority, it blossoms anew at the Griffin's touch.
A name for the constellation Pisces; Dante uses it astronomically to mark the spring season when trees bud and bloom.
The nymph whose tale, told by Mercury, lulled the hundred-eyed Argus to sleep so he could be slain; Dante compares his own falling asleep in Eden to those drowsing eyes.
The three apostles present at the Transfiguration, dazzled and then restored by Christ's word; Dante likens his waking in Eden to their awakening on the mountain.
The Old Testament prophet who appeared with Moses at Christ's Transfiguration and then was gone; named in the simile for Dante's waking in Eden.
The eagle, Jupiter's bird; it plunges through the tree and strikes the chariot, figuring the persecutions or assaults the Church suffered (often read as the Roman emperors).
In the chariot's transformation, a starved fox leaps into the car and is driven off by Beatrice; it figures heresy assailing the Church.
In the chariot's transformation, a dragon rises from the split ground and tears away part of the car with its tail; it figures Satan or a deep wound to the Church.
The shameless prostitute who rides the transformed, monstrous chariot, kissing the giant beside her; she figures the corrupted Church (or papacy) gone whoring after worldly power.
The giant who guards the harlot on the chariot and then beats and drags her off; he figures the French monarchy (the house of France) and its grip on the papacy.
Latin, 'O God, the nations have come' (Psalm 79), the lament the seven ladies sing over the ravaged chariot.
The Virgin Mary grieving at the crucifixion; Beatrice's sorrow over the wrecked chariot is said to be scarcely less than Mary's at the cross.
Latin, 'A little while, and you shall not see me' (John 16), Christ's words to his disciples, spoken by Beatrice to foretell change and return after the Church's trial.
The poet Statius, who remains with Dante after Virgil has departed and follows Beatrice through the Earthly Paradise.
Beatrice's coded prophecy of a coming deliverer (the Roman numerals DXV, often read as DUX, 'leader') sent by God to kill the harlot and the giant and reform the Church.
The monster of Thebes whose riddle baffled all comers; Beatrice compares her own dark prophecy to the Sphinx's puzzling speech.
The Greek goddess of divine law and oracles, known for obscure pronouncements; Beatrice links her riddling prophecy to Themis as well as the Sphinx.
Water-nymphs; in the classical version Beatrice alludes to, they solved the Sphinx's riddle. She says future events themselves will be the 'Naiads' that unriddle her dark words.
An Italian river whose mineral waters coat and petrify objects left in them; Beatrice says vain thoughts have 'stone-stilled' Dante's mind like the water of Elsa.
One of the two rivers Dante seems to see rising from a single spring in Eden (with the Tigris); Beatrice identifies them as the one stream Lethe and Eunoë.
One of the two rivers Dante seems to see flowing from a single source in Eden, parting like reluctant friends; revealed to be Lethe and Eunoë.
The sun, whose rising at a particularly favorable point (where four circles meet in three crosses) Dante uses to set the season and hour as Paradiso begins.
The wreath of bay leaves awarded to triumphant poets and emperors, sacred to Apollo; Dante hopes to earn it with this final part of his poem.
